Interactive module

Java Intermediate

The modern language and library — generics in depth, lambdas and streams, records, sealed types and pattern matching, Optional, java.time and NIO — applied to the same order-and-inventory system, now grown into a pricing and reporting pipeline.

Intermediate Java 21 LTS 9–11 hours Updated October 2026

Start here

How to use this module

Work through it at your own pace. Your section checkmarks, quiz answers, flashcard marks and notes are saved in this browser under a key scoped to this file, so closing the tab loses nothing and Java Fundamentals cannot overwrite it. Nothing is sent anywhere — this page makes no network requests at all. Press ? at any time for the keyboard shortcuts, and use Reset progress in the sidebar to start over.

Every code sample in this module was compiled and executed against a real JDK 21 as part of the build. If an Expected output block appears under a program, that text is what the program actually printed, not what it ought to print. Where a widget animates execution rather than reporting it — the step-through of how a stream pulls elements, or how javac erases a type argument — it is labelled Simulated. Java cannot run in a browser, and this module does not pretend otherwise.

The same warehouse, grown up

Fundamentals built a small inventory system: a Product with a SKU and a price, an Order of OrderLines, and an InventoryService. This module keeps every one of those types and rewrites them with the tools it teaches:

  • Product gains a Category enum with per-constant behaviour (§3), and the catalogue is queried with streams (§5).
  • Order and OrderLine become records (§8), validated in compact constructors and used as map keys without a hand-written equals.
  • A sealed Discount family — percentage, fixed amount, buy-N-get-one — is priced with an exhaustive pattern switch (§9).
  • A reporting pipeline groups revenue by category with collectors (§6), ranks products with comparators (§10), filters by date with java.time (§12) and writes the result with java.nio.file (§13).

Before you begin

Prerequisites

This module assumes Java Fundamentals, or the equivalent: you can already write a class, a loop and a try block in Java without looking anything up. Each item below is something it builds on directly, with the Fundamentals section that taught it:

Prerequisite skills, where they were taught, and what depends on them here
You should already be able to…Taught inBecause this module…
Implement equals and hashCode as a matched pairFundamentals §10shows what records generate for you, and why a mutable key breaks a HashMap
Declare and consume a List<Product>, and say what erasure meansFundamentals §13goes straight to wildcards, bounds and the limits erasure imposes
Explain dynamic dispatch and the overload-resolution phasesFundamentals §7, §8leans on both to explain how lambdas find their target type and how default methods resolve

What you need installed

A JDK 21 or newer. This is not negotiable in the way it was for Fundamentals: records (16), sealed types (17), pattern matching for switch and record patterns (21) are all used as ordinary language here, and an older compiler rejects the examples outright. No IDE is required.

java -version    # expect: openjdk version "21.x" or newer
javac -version   # must match; a mismatched pair causes "class file has wrong version"

If you see UnsupportedClassVersionError when running, your java is older than your javac. Check PATH and JAVA_HOME point at the same installation.

If you skipped Fundamentals

Four ideas carry most of the weight here. If any of these sentences is not obviously true to you, read the Fundamentals section first — it is a twenty-minute detour that saves an hour of confusion.

  • The equals/hashCode contract. Two objects that are equals must return the same hashCode, or every hash-based collection silently misfiles them. Records (§8) exist largely so you stop writing this by hand; HashMap internals (§11) show what goes wrong when the hash changes after insertion.
  • Erasure. List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime. §1 starts from that fact and derives everything generics can and cannot do.
  • Dynamic dispatch versus static resolution. The JVM picks an override from the runtime class; the compiler picks an overload from the declared types. Lambdas (§4) and default methods (§3) each sit on one side of that line.
  • Try-with-resources. A resource acquired in the header is closed in reverse order, always. A Stream from Files.lines (§13) is such a resource, and forgetting that leaks a file handle.

The contract

Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to do each of the following without reaching for a reference. The final quiz tests exactly these twelve.

  1. Choose the wildcard (? extends, ? super, unbounded, or none) for a given API from the PECS rule, and explain what erasure prevents.
  2. Distinguish static nested, inner, local and anonymous classes, and state what each can capture and why the captured variable must be effectively final.
  3. Resolve which default method wins when a class inherits two, and design an enum with per-constant behaviour.
  4. Convert any lambda to a method reference (and back), name its functional interface, and predict what this means inside each.
  5. Trace a stream pipeline element by element — laziness, short-circuiting and stateful operations — and say which operations force a full pass.
  6. Build a groupingBy with a downstream collector, and choose between toMap merge strategies.
  7. Use Optional as a return type without get(), and name the three places it should never appear.
  8. Write a record with a validating compact constructor, and explain why its immutability is shallow.
  9. Model a closed hierarchy with sealed and consume it with an exhaustive pattern switch that needs no default.
  10. Explain what HashMap does on resize, why a mutable key breaks it, and the difference between an unmodifiable view and an immutable copy.
  11. Compute with java.time correctly across a DST change, and choose Duration versus Period.
  12. Read and write files with java.nio.file using an explicit charset and a stream that is always closed.
Deliberately out of scope

Threads and the Java memory model, locks and concurrent collections, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, garbage collection and JVM tuning, class loading, reflection and annotation processing, the module system and JNI all belong to Java Advanced. Parallel streams are mentioned in §5 only to say when not to use them; the reasons why belong to the memory-model material there. Everything in this module is single-threaded on purpose, so that the behaviour you observe is the behaviour of the language, not of a scheduler.

Section 1

Generics in depth

Fundamentals left generics at the point where you can declare a List<Product> and get a Product back without a cast. That is the consumer's view. This section is the designer's view: how to write a method or class that works for a whole family of types, and why the rules that make that safe produce some of the strangest-looking signatures in the JDK.

Everything follows from one decision made in 2004: generic type arguments exist only at compile time. The compiler checks them, then erases them, and the bytecode that runs contains plain List, plain Object, and a cast wherever you read an element out. Every limitation in this section — no new T(), no List<int>, no instanceof List<String> — is a direct consequence of that.

Invariance: why a List<Perishable> is not a List<Product>

A Perishable is a Product. It is natural to assume a List<Perishable> is therefore a List<Product>, and the compiler says no. Here is why it must:

List<Perishable> dairy = new ArrayList<>();
List<Product> products = dairy;              // if this were allowed…
products.add(new Product("GIRD-1", 120_000)); // …a girder would land in the dairy list
Perishable p = dairy.get(0);                 // and this would throw ClassCastException

Generic types are invariant: List<A> and List<B> are unrelated no matter how A and B relate. Arrays, designed a decade earlier, went the other way — Perishable[] is a Product[] — and pay for it at runtime with ArrayStoreException, which the language designers regarded as a mistake not to repeat. Invariance is safe but inconvenient: a method taking List<Product> cannot accept the dairy list even to read it. Wildcards are the fix.

Wildcards and PECS

A wildcard loosens the type argument in one direction. List<? extends Product> means "a list of some unknown subtype of Product"; List<? super Perishable> means "a list of some unknown supertype of Perishable". Which one you want depends entirely on whether the method reads or writes, and the mnemonic is PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

javaPecs.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Pecs {
 
    static class Product {
        final String sku; final int priceInCents;
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku; }
    }
    static class Perishable extends Product {
        final int shelfDays;
        Perishable(String sku, int priceInCents, int shelfDays) { super(sku, priceInCents); this.shelfDays = shelfDays; }
    }
 
    // PRODUCER: we only READ Products out of `src`, so accept any List of a subtype
    static int totalInCents(List<? extends Product> src) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (Product p : src) sum += p.priceInCents;   // reading as Product is always safe
        return sum;
    }
 
    // CONSUMER: we only WRITE Perishables into `dst`, so accept any List of a supertype
    static void restockPerishables(List<? super Perishable> dst) {
        dst.add(new Perishable("MILK-1", 120, 7));      // writing a Perishable is always safe
        dst.add(new Perishable("EGGS-6", 240, 21));
    }
 
    // BOTH: reads and writes, so the type must be exact — no wildcard
    static void swapFirstTwo(List<Product> list) {
        Product first = list.get(0);
        list.set(0, list.get(1));
        list.set(1, first);
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Perishable> dairy = new ArrayList<>();
        restockPerishables(dairy);                      // List<Perishable> is a List<? super Perishable>
        System.out.println("dairy         = " + dairy);
 
        List<Product> catalogue = new ArrayList<>();
        catalogue.add(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
        catalogue.add(new Product("GIRD-1", 120_000));
        restockPerishables(catalogue);                  // List<Product> is ALSO a List<? super Perishable>
        System.out.println("catalogue     = " + catalogue);
 
        System.out.println("total(dairy)  = " + totalInCents(dairy));       // List<Perishable> as a producer
        System.out.println("total(catal.) = " + totalInCents(catalogue));   // List<Product> as a producer
 
        List<Object> anything = new ArrayList<>();
        restockPerishables(anything);                   // even List<Object> is a List<? super Perishable>
        System.out.println("anything      = " + anything);
 
        swapFirstTwo(catalogue);
        System.out.println("swapped       = " + catalogue);
 
        // totalInCents(anything);                       // does not compile: Object is not a Product
        // restockPerishables(new ArrayList<String>());  // does not compile: String is not a supertype
    }
}
Expected output
dairy         = [MILK-1, EGGS-6]
catalogue     = [BOLT-7, GIRD-1, MILK-1, EGGS-6]
total(dairy)  = 360
total(catal.) = 120440
anything      = [MILK-1, EGGS-6]
swapped       = [GIRD-1, BOLT-7, MILK-1, EGGS-6]

Read the three signatures as promises. totalInCents promises never to add anything, so it can be handed a list of anything that is at least a Product. restockPerishables promises only ever to add Perishables, so it can be handed any list those will fit in — and a List<Object> qualifies. swapFirstTwo does both and so can promise neither; its parameter is exact. The wildcards buy flexibility for the caller at the price of restrictions inside the method, which the compiler enforces: try to add to a ? extends list, or read a typed element from a ? super list, and it refuses.

Pick the wildcard

What does your method do with the list?

Match each parameter type to its job

Drag a type onto its slot, or click one then click the other

Each slot describes what a method does with a List parameter. Place the element type that fits.

All four correct. Summing reads only — producer, extends. Adding writes only — consumer, super. isEmpty() touches no element — unbounded. Replacing reads each element and writes one back — exact type, or a generic method <T extends Product> void discount(List<T>).

Bounded type parameters and generic methods

A wildcard constrains an argument you receive. A type parameter — the <T> before a method's return type — names an unknown type so you can refer to it more than once: take a List<T>, return a T. A bound on it (T extends Something) is what lets you call methods on a T; without a bound, all the compiler knows is that T is an Object.

javaBounds.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Bounds {
 
    static class Product implements Comparable<Product> {
        final String sku; final int priceInCents;
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @Override public int compareTo(Product o) { return Integer.compare(priceInCents, o.priceInCents); }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents; }
    }
    interface Stockable { int onHand(); }
 
    // Perishable inherits compareTo(Product): it is Comparable<Product>, NOT Comparable<Perishable>
    static class Perishable extends Product implements Stockable {
        final int onHand;
        Perishable(String sku, int priceInCents, int onHand) { super(sku, priceInCents); this.onHand = onHand; }
        @Override public int onHand() { return onHand; }
    }
 
    // Bounded type parameter. Without `? super T`, max(dairy) below would not compile,
    // because Perishable is only Comparable<Product>, never Comparable<Perishable>.
    static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(List<T> items) {
        T best = items.get(0);
        for (T t : items) if (t.compareTo(best) > 0) best = t;
        return best;
    }
 
    // Generic method: T is inferred from the arguments, the caller never writes <Product>
    static <T> List<T> pair(T a, T b) {
        List<T> out = new ArrayList<>();
        out.add(a); out.add(b);
        return out;
    }
 
    // Intersection bound: T must be a Product AND Stockable. The class comes first, then interfaces.
    // Inside, every T has both priceInCents and onHand() — no cast, no instanceof.
    static <T extends Product & Stockable> int stockValueInCents(List<T> items) {
        int total = 0;
        for (T t : items) total += t.priceInCents * t.onHand();
        return total;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Perishable> dairy = List.of(new Perishable("MILK-1", 120, 40), new Perishable("EGGS-6", 240, 12), new Perishable("BUTR-2", 310, 5));
        List<Product> parts = List.of(new Product("BOLT-7", 80), new Product("GIRD-1", 120_000), new Product("NUT-3", 25));
 
        System.out.println("max(dairy)      = " + max(dairy));      // T = Perishable; bound met via Comparable<Product>
        System.out.println("max(parts)      = " + max(parts));
        System.out.println("stock value     = " + stockValueInCents(dairy));   // T = Perishable satisfies both bounds
        // stockValueInCents(parts);   // does not compile: Product is not Stockable
 
        List<Product> two = pair(new Product("A", 1), new Product("B", 2));   // T inferred as Product
        List<Object> mixed = pair("BOLT-7", 42);                              // T inferred as Object (see below)
        System.out.println("pair            = " + two + " / " + mixed);
 
        // A Comparator supplies ordering from outside; List.sort takes Comparator<? super E>,
        // so a Comparator<Product> sorts a List<Perishable>
        Comparator<Product> bySku = Comparator.comparing(p -> p.sku);
        List<Perishable> sorted = new ArrayList<>(dairy);
        sorted.sort(bySku);
        System.out.println("sorted by sku   = " + sorted);
 
        System.out.println("max(strings)    = " + max(List.of("BOLT", "NUT", "CAM")));  // String is Comparable<String>
    }
}
Expected output
max(dairy)      = BUTR-2@310
max(parts)      = GIRD-1@120000
stock value     = 9230
pair            = [A@1, B@2] / [BOLT-7, 42]
sorted by sku   = [BUTR-2@310, EGGS-6@240, MILK-1@120]
max(strings)    = NUT

Three things in that program are worth slowing down for.

  • The recursive bound T extends Comparable<? super T>. The obvious version, T extends Comparable<T>, rejects max(dairy): Perishable inherited compareTo(Product) and so implements Comparable<Product>, not Comparable<Perishable>. The ? super says "comparable to itself or to something more general", which is exactly the PECS rule again — the comparator consumes a T. This is the signature of Collections.max, Collections.sort and every sorted() in the JDK.
  • Inference. Nobody writes Bounds.<Product>pair(…). The compiler infers T from the arguments and, since Java 8, from the target too: pair("BOLT-7", 42) on its own would infer an unpronounceable intersection of Serializable and Comparable, but assigned to a List<Object> it infers Object because that is what the assignment needs.
  • Intersection bounds. T extends Product & Stockable gives you both APIs on every T with no cast. One class at most, listed first; any number of interfaces after it. You cannot write T extends Product & Comparable<? super T> here, because Product already fixes Comparable<Product> and the compiler rejects "Comparable cannot be inherited with different arguments".

Compiler notes

What erasure forbids, and what to do instead

Things erasure prevents, why, and the workaround
You cannot writeBecause at runtimeInstead
new T()T is Object; there is no constructor to callPass a Supplier<T> (§4) or a Class<T> token
new T[n]the array would be an Object[] and lie about its type(T[]) new Object[n] kept private, or better, an ArrayList<T>
x instanceof List<String>every List is the same classx instanceof List<?>, then trust the declared type
List<int>int is not an ObjectList<Integer>, or IntStream / int[] when boxing costs matter

Generics gotchas
  • A wildcard in a return type helps nobody. List<? extends Product> find() forces every caller to deal with the wildcard. Use wildcards in parameters; return the exact type.
  • List<?> and raw List are not the same. The wildcard is a typed "list of something" and still forbids unsafe adds. The raw type switches off generics entirely and produces the unchecked warnings Fundamentals §13 showed you. -Xlint:rawtypes -Werror turns the difference into a build failure.
  • "Capture of ?" in an error message is not a bug in the compiler. Each use of a wildcard is given a fresh, anonymous type variable (CAP#1); the message is telling you that it cannot prove two of them are the same. The fix is usually a small private generic helper method that gives the capture a name: private static <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l) called from swap(List<?> l).
  • Bounds are not implemented by subtypes automatically. Perishable extends Product implements Comparable<Product> never becomes Comparable<Perishable>. That is why the ? super T appears in every sorting signature, and why forgetting it produces an error that mentions neither sorting nor subclasses.
  • @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") is a promise, not a fix. Put it on the smallest scope possible, with a comment proving why the cast is safe. An unchecked cast that is wrong does not fail where you wrote it — it fails at some later get, in code that looks innocent.

Check yourself

1.List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>(); does not compile. What is the compiler protecting you from?

C. If the assignment were legal, nums.add(2.5) would type-check (a Double is a Number) and corrupt the Integer list; the failure would surface later, as a ClassCastException at some unrelated get. Invariance moves that error to compile time, at the line that caused it.

A is backwards — reading an Integer as a Number is always safe and is exactly what List<? extends Number> permits. B is wrong: arrays do allow the equivalent assignment and pay for it with ArrayStoreException at runtime, which is the problem generics were designed not to repeat. D cannot happen because the assignment is rejected before any code runs.

2.Given static void copy(List<? super Product> dst, List<? extends Product> src), which calls compile? Select all that apply.

A and C. The destination must hold Product or a supertype; the source must supply Product or a subtype. A: Object is a supertype of Product and Perishable is a subtype — both bounds satisfied. C: the exact type satisfies both wildcards trivially.

B fails on the first argument: Perishable is a subtype of Product, so a List<Perishable> is not a List<? super Product> — the method could put a non-perishable Product into it. D fails on the second: a List<Object> might contain a String, so it is not a List<? extends Product>. This is the signature of Collections.copy, and it is the clearest illustration of PECS in the JDK.

3.Inside static <T> T blank(), the line return new T(); is rejected. What is the root cause?

B. The bytecode for blank() is compiled once and contains no T — the JVM would have to construct "an Object", which is useless. The standard fixes both pass the missing information in explicitly: a Supplier<T> such as Product::new, or a Class<T> token and clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance().

A is a real concern but not the cause — C# has reified generics and solves it with a new() constraint; Java cannot because the information is gone. C is false: new ArrayList<T>() inside a generic method is fine, because ArrayList is a real class. D describes a different, solvable problem: T is inferred from the assignment target, as in Product p = blank();.

Section 2

Nested, inner, local and anonymous classes

Java lets you declare a class inside another class, inside a method, or inside an expression. The four forms look similar and are not: they differ in what they can see, what they secretly hold a reference to, and when they are the right tool. Lambdas (§4) are the fifth member of the family, and most of what makes them simple is that they drop the baggage described here.

The question to ask of any nested class is: does it need an instance of the enclosing class to exist? If not, it is static and is merely a class that lives in a namespace. If so, it is inner, and every one of its instances carries a hidden pointer to the outer instance that created it.

Worked example

javaNested.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Nested {
 
    // 1. STATIC NESTED: a class placed inside another for namespacing. No outer instance.
    static class Line {
        final String sku; final int qty;
        Line(String sku, int qty) { this.sku = sku; this.qty = qty; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "x" + qty; }
    }
 
    private final List<Line> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    private final String orderId;
 
    Nested(String orderId) { this.orderId = orderId; }
 
    // 2. INNER: every instance carries a hidden reference to the enclosing Nested (Nested.this)
    class Cursor {
        private int pos = 0;                                       // the cursor's own state
        boolean hasNext() { return pos < lines.size(); }           // `lines` means Nested.this.lines
        Line next() { return lines.get(pos++); }
        String owner() { return Nested.this.orderId; }             // the qualified form, written out
    }
 
    Cursor cursor() { return new Cursor(); }                       // `this` becomes the new Cursor's outer
 
    int totalQty() {
        int base = 100;                                            // a local that a local class will capture
 
        // 3. LOCAL: declared inside a method; sees the method's effectively-final locals
        class Counter {
            int sum = base;                                        // `base` is COPIED into the Counter at construction
            void add(Line l) { sum += l.qty; }
        }
        Counter c = new Counter();
        for (Line l : lines) c.add(l);
        // base = 0;   // uncomment: "local variables referenced from an inner class must be final or effectively final"
        return c.sum - base;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Nested order = new Nested("ORD-1");
        order.lines.add(new Line("BOLT-7", 3));
        order.lines.add(new Line("NUT-3", 10));
 
        Line standalone = new Nested.Line("CAM-9", 1);             // static nested: no outer instance needed
        System.out.println("static nested = " + standalone);
 
        Nested.Cursor cur = order.cursor();                        // inner: created THROUGH an instance
        Nested.Cursor other = order.new Cursor();                  // the explicit (and rarely seen) form
        System.out.println("inner owner   = " + cur.owner() + " / " + other.owner());
        StringBuilder walked = new StringBuilder();
        while (cur.hasNext()) walked.append(cur.next()).append(' ');
        System.out.println("walked        = " + walked.toString().trim());
 
        System.out.println("local class   = " + order.totalQty());
 
        // 4. ANONYMOUS: a one-off implementation declared at the point of use
        Runnable report = new Runnable() {
            @Override public void run() {
                // `this` here is the anonymous Runnable itself, never the enclosing class
                System.out.println("anonymous     = this is a " + this.getClass().getSuperclass().getSimpleName()
                        + ", simple name '" + this.getClass().getSimpleName() + "'");
            }
        };
        report.run();
 
        // A lambda has no `this` of its own; it captures the enclosing instance's, if there is one
        Runnable lambda = () -> System.out.println("lambda        = " + order.lines.size() + " lines captured");
        lambda.run();
    }
}
Expected output
static nested = CAM-9x1
inner owner   = ORD-1 / ORD-1
walked        = BOLT-7x3 NUT-3x10
local class   = 13
anonymous     = this is a Object, simple name ''
lambda        = 2 lines captured

Line is static: it is a value type that happens to be scoped under Nested, and new Nested.Line(…) needs no order to exist. Cursor is inner: lines inside it is really Nested.this.lines, resolved through a hidden field the compiler added, which is why it can only be created from an instance — order.cursor(), or the explicit order.new Cursor(). Counter is local to one method and copies the local base into itself. The anonymous Runnable is a class with no name (getSimpleName() is empty) whose superclass is Object, because Runnable is an interface.

The four forms side by side

public class Order {
    public static class Line { … }      // Order.Line — a top-level class in all but name
}
Order.Line l = new Order.Line("BOLT-7", 3);
  • Sees: the outer class's static members, including private ones. No outer instance.
  • Holds: nothing extra. Same memory footprint as a top-level class.
  • Use for: helper types that belong with their owner — a builder, a node, a value type like Map.Entry. Default to this form.
public class Order {
    private final List<Line> lines = …;
    public class Cursor {               // no `static`: each Cursor has an Order.this
        Line next() { return lines.get(pos++); }
    }
}
Order.Cursor c = order.new Cursor();    // or, far more usually, a method on Order that does this
  • Sees: everything in the outer instance, as if it were written inside it. Name clashes are resolved with Order.this.field.
  • Holds: a synthetic final Order this$0 field, set by a constructor parameter you never see. The outer object cannot be garbage-collected while the inner one lives.
  • Use for: iterators, cursors and views that are meaningless without their owner. ArrayList.Itr is an inner class for exactly this reason.
int totalQty() {
    int base = 100;                     // must be effectively final to be captured
    class Counter {
        int sum = base;                 // reads a COPY, taken when the Counter is constructed
    }
    return new Counter().sum;
}
  • Sees: the enclosing instance (if the method is not static) plus the method's locals and parameters — but only those that are never reassigned.
  • Holds: the outer this (in an instance method) and a private copy of each captured local, as synthetic val$base fields.
  • Use for: rarely. A local record or enum (§8) is the modern reason to reach for this form: a throwaway tuple scoped to one method.
Comparator<Line> byQty = new Comparator<Line>() {   // declares AND instantiates a subclass
    @Override public int compare(Line a, Line b) { return Integer.compare(a.qty, b.qty); }
};
// since Java 8, for a single-method interface, write a lambda instead:
Comparator<Line> byQty2 = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.qty, b.qty);
  • Sees: the same as a local class. Same capture rules.
  • Holds: the same hidden fields as a local class. this inside it is the anonymous object, so this.toString() is its toString, not the outer one.
  • Use for: implementing an interface with more than one abstract method, or subclassing a class, at the point of use. For a single abstract method, a lambda is shorter, clearer, and does not allocate a class.

Watch a local get captured

Why the captured variable must be effectively final Simulated ← → to step
Source
int totalQty() {
    int base = 100;
    class Counter {
        int sum = base;
        void add(int q) { sum += q; }
    }
    Counter c = new Counter();
    c.add(3);
    c.add(10);
    // base = 0;   <- would not compile
    return c.sum - base;
}
Two places the value lives
Standard output
Nested-class gotchas
  • An inner class keeps its outer alive. Register an inner-class listener with a long-lived registry and the whole enclosing object — and everything it references — cannot be collected until the listener is removed. This is the classic Android and Swing memory leak. If the nested class does not use the outer instance, make it static; the compiler will tell you nothing is broken, and -Xlint stays silent too.
  • Serialising an inner class serialises its outer. The hidden this$0 is a field like any other, so the enclosing object goes to the stream too — and if it is not Serializable, you get a NotSerializableException naming a class you never asked to serialise.
  • this means different things in an anonymous class and a lambda. In the anonymous class it is the anonymous object; in a lambda it is the enclosing instance. Converting one to the other changes the meaning of every this and every unqualified call to an inherited method — IDEs warn, but only if you read the warning.
  • Shadowing is silent. An inner class field named lines hides the outer lines for the whole inner body. Reach past it with Outer.this.lines. A lambda, by contrast, cannot shadow a local — redeclaring base as a lambda parameter is a compile error — which is one reason lambdas are easier to read.
  • Effectively final is checked per variable, not per use. A single i++ anywhere in the method, even after the capture, makes i uncapturable everywhere. The error points at the capture, not at the increment.

Check yourself

1.This method does not compile. What is the smallest change that fixes it while still counting?
int count = 0; lines.forEach(l -> { if (l.qty() > 5) count++; }); return count;

D. The lambda captures count by copy, so count++ inside it could only ever increment the copy — which is why the compiler rejects it rather than let it silently do nothing. The honest fixes stop mutating a captured local: a loop, or a stream that produces the count as its result.

A makes the problem worse — a final variable cannot be incremented anywhere. B is false: anonymous classes have exactly the same capture rule as lambdas. C compiles, and is wrong in a way the compiler cannot see: a static field is shared by every call on every thread, so two concurrent counts corrupt each other. The int[1] or AtomicInteger trick also compiles, but exists mainly to work around the rule in callbacks you cannot restructure.

2.Inside an instance method of Order, you replace new Runnable() { public void run() { log(this.toString()); } } with () -> log(this.toString()). What changes?

B. An anonymous class is a real object with its own this; a lambda is not, so this inside it is lexically the enclosing instance — the Order. The behaviour changes from logging something like Order$1@1b6d3586 to logging the order itself.

A is the common assumption and the reason this refactoring is a known trap. C is wrong: this is legal in a lambda inside an instance method; it is illegal only in a static context, where there is no instance at all. D invents a rule — this is captured at creation like any other value.

3.A code review flags class Builder nested inside Order because it is not static, although it never touches an Order field. Which consequences of leaving it non-static are real? Select all that apply.

A and D. A non-static nested class is inner, full stop: it gets a this$0 field whether or not the body uses it (A), and it can only be instantiated through an existing outer instance (D) — which for a builder, whose whole purpose is to exist before the Order, is absurd. The fix is one keyword.

B is what you would hope for, but javac and -Xlint:all say nothing; only IDE inspections catch it. C is not real — the extra field costs memory and retention, not time.

Section 3

Interfaces and enums in depth

Fundamentals §8 drew the line between an abstract class and an interface: state on one side, pure contract on the other. That line moved in Java 8. An interface can now ship behaviour — default methods with bodies, static factories, and since Java 9 private helpers — while still carrying no instance state. The reason was pragmatic: Collection.stream() had to be added to an interface that thousands of third-party classes already implemented, without breaking a single one of them. A method with a body that implementers inherit automatically was the only way.

That convenience creates one genuinely new problem — a class can now inherit two bodies for the same method — and the language resolves it with three rules you need to know by heart. The second half of this section does the same for enum, which is far more than a list of names: each constant is a singleton object that can carry fields, constructors, and its own method bodies.

Four kinds of interface method

Interface member kinds, their modifiers and what they are for
KindWritten asImplementers getUse it for
Abstractint priceInCents();an obligation — implicitly public abstractthe contract itself
Defaultdefault String describe() { … }a body they may keep or overrideevolving a published interface; convenience built on the abstract methods
Staticstatic Priced of(int c) { … }nothing — called only as Priced.of(…), never inheritedfactories and utilities that belong with the type
Privateprivate int handling() { … }nothing — invisible outside the interfacesharing code between two defaults without exposing it

A field in an interface is always public static final whether you write the modifiers or not. It is a constant, not state — an interface still has no instance fields and never will.

Worked example: all three resolution rules

Three classes, each inheriting describe() from more than one place. The output shows which body ran and the comments name the rule that chose it.

javaDefaultMethods.java
public class DefaultMethods {
 
    interface Priced {
        int priceInCents();
        default String describe() { return "priced at " + priceInCents() + "c"; }
        static Priced of(int cents) { return () -> cents; }        // static: called as Priced.of(...)
    }
 
    interface Shippable {
        int shippingInCents();
        default String describe() { return "ships for " + shippingInCents() + "c"; }
        default int totalInCents(int price) { return price + shippingInCents() + handling(); }
        private int handling() { return 50; }                        // private: shared by defaults only
    }
 
    // rule 3: two unrelated defaults with one signature -> the class MUST override
    static class Bolt implements Priced, Shippable {
        public int priceInCents() { return 80; }
        public int shippingInCents() { return 150; }
        @Override public String describe() {
            return Priced.super.describe() + ", " + Shippable.super.describe();
        }
    }
 
    interface Fragile extends Shippable {
        @Override default String describe() { return "fragile: " + Shippable.super.describe(); }
    }
    // rule 2: the more specific interface wins -> Fragile's default, not Shippable's
    static class Lens implements Shippable, Fragile {
        public int shippingInCents() { return 900; }
    }
 
    static class Base { public String describe() { return "a plain class method"; } }
    // rule 1: a superclass method always beats an interface default
    static class Girder extends Base implements Priced {
        public int priceInCents() { return 120_000; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Bolt:   " + new Bolt().describe());
        System.out.println("Lens:   " + new Lens().describe());
        System.out.println("Girder: " + new Girder().describe());
        System.out.println("total:  " + new Lens().totalInCents(1_000));
        System.out.println("static: " + Priced.of(25).describe());
    }
}
Expected output
Bolt:   priced at 80c, ships for 150c
Lens:   fragile: ships for 900c
Girder: a plain class method
total:  1950
static: priced at 25c

The rules, in the order the compiler applies them:

  1. A class wins over any interface. If a superclass — however far up — supplies a concrete method, every interface default with that signature is ignored. Girder prints Base's text and Priced.describe never runs. This is what keeps old code old: adding a default to an interface cannot change what an existing class hierarchy does.
  2. A more specific interface wins over a less specific one. Fragile extends Shippable and overrides the default, so for Lens the Fragile body is chosen even though Lens names Shippable first. Declaration order is irrelevant.
  3. Otherwise the class must decide. Priced and Shippable are unrelated and both supply describe(). Delete Bolt's override and the compiler says class Bolt inherits unrelated defaults for describe() from types Priced and Shippable. The override may do anything, including delegate to one or both with the Interface.super.method() syntax — the only place that form is legal.

Note the private helper: handling() is callable from totalInCents but not from Lens, so the interface can factor out shared logic without widening its public surface.

Resolve a diamond yourself

Which describe() does new Bolt().describe() run?

Choose where describe() is defined. Bolt extends Base implements Priced, Shippable, and Bolt itself has no override.

Functional interfaces, briefly

An interface with exactly one abstract method — default, static and private methods do not count — is a functional interface, and that single method is what a lambda implements. Priced above qualifies, which is why Priced.of could return () -> cents. Comparator, Runnable and everything in java.util.function are functional interfaces. §4 is about nothing else.

Enums are classes

An enum declares a class with a fixed, compiler-known set of instances. Each constant is created once, during class initialisation, by calling the enum's constructor — which is why that constructor is always private and why == is the correct way to compare enum values. Everything a class can have, an enum can have: fields, methods, constructors, interfaces, and even a different method body per constant.

javaEnums.java
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Map;
 
public class Enums {
 
    interface Describable { String describe(); }
 
    enum Category implements Describable {
        FASTENER("Fasteners", 1.0) {
            @Override int shippingInCents(int weightGrams) { return 150; }            // flat rate
        },
        STRUCTURAL("Structural steel", 2.5) {
            @Override int shippingInCents(int weightGrams) { return weightGrams * 3; }
        },
        TOOLING("Tooling", 1.2) {
            @Override int shippingInCents(int weightGrams) { return 500 + weightGrams; }
        };
 
        private final String label;
        private final double multiplier;
 
        Category(String label, double multiplier) {      // always private: nobody else can call new
            this.label = label;
            this.multiplier = multiplier;
        }
 
        abstract int shippingInCents(int weightGrams);   // every constant must supply a body
 
        String label() { return label; }
        double multiplier() { return multiplier; }
 
        @Override public String describe() { return label + " (x" + multiplier + ")"; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Category c : Category.values()) {
            System.out.printf("%-10s ordinal=%d  %-22s ship(200g)=%d%n",
                    c, c.ordinal(), c.describe(), c.shippingInCents(200));
        }
 
        Category parsed = Category.valueOf("TOOLING");
        System.out.println("valueOf -> " + parsed + ", same object: " + (parsed == Category.TOOLING));
 
        Map<Category, Integer> stockByCategory = new EnumMap<>(Category.class);
        stockByCategory.put(Category.TOOLING, 4);
        stockByCategory.put(Category.FASTENER, 1_200);
        System.out.println("EnumMap keeps declaration order: " + stockByCategory);
 
        EnumSet<Category> heavy = EnumSet.of(Category.STRUCTURAL, Category.TOOLING);
        System.out.println("complement of " + heavy + " is " + EnumSet.complementOf(heavy));
 
        String storage = switch (parsed) {               // exhaustive: no default needed
            case FASTENER   -> "bin";
            case STRUCTURAL -> "yard";
            case TOOLING    -> "locked cage";
        };
        System.out.println("switch -> " + storage);
 
        try {
            Category.valueOf("tooling");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("valueOf is exact-match only: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Expected output
FASTENER   ordinal=0  Fasteners (x1.0)       ship(200g)=150
STRUCTURAL ordinal=1  Structural steel (x2.5) ship(200g)=600
TOOLING    ordinal=2  Tooling (x1.2)         ship(200g)=700
valueOf -> TOOLING, same object: true
EnumMap keeps declaration order: {FASTENER=1200, TOOLING=4}
complement of [STRUCTURAL, TOOLING] is [FASTENER]
switch -> locked cage
valueOf is exact-match only: No enum constant Enums.Category.tooling

Three things in that program deserve a closer look.

Writing { … } after a constant's arguments creates an anonymous subclass of the enum for that one constant. An abstract method on the enum then forces every constant to supply its own body, and the compiler refuses a new constant that forgets. This replaces the switch (this) inside a method that silently falls through when someone adds a constant — the behaviour lives next to the data it belongs to.

The cost is that FASTENER.getClass() is a subclass, not Category itself. Use getDeclaringClass() if you ever need the enum type reflectively.

An enum has a known number of constants, each with a fixed ordinal(). EnumMap exploits that: it is an array indexed by ordinal, so get and put are a single array access with no hashing, no boxing and no collisions, and iteration is always in declaration order. EnumSet is a bit vector — one long for up to 64 constants — which makes contains, union and complementOf single machine instructions.

Prefer them over HashMap/HashSet whenever the key is an enum. They are also the right way to represent a set of flags; a bit-mask int is what they replace.

Inside a switch on an enum you write the bare constant name — case TOOLING, not case Category.TOOLING. The compiler knows the type from the selector. A switch expression (the arrow form that yields a value) must be exhaustive: cover every constant and you need no default, and adding a fourth constant later becomes a compile error at every such switch rather than a silent fall-through. §9 takes this further with sealed types.

Avoid writing a default in an enum switch expression that could be exhaustive. It compiles today, and it hides tomorrow's missing case.

Gotchas
  • Never persist ordinal(). It is the constant's position in the source file. Insert a constant in the middle and every stored number now means something else. Store name(), or an explicit field such as a database code, and look it up on the way back in.
  • valueOf is exact and throws. It compares the full name, case-sensitively, and raises IllegalArgumentException — not null — on a miss. User input needs a guard: normalise it, or loop over values() comparing with equalsIgnoreCase.
  • A default method cannot override Object methods. default String toString() in an interface is a compile error. Every class already has one from Object, and rule 1 says the class would win anyway.
  • Defaults do not let an interface hold state. A default method can only call other interface methods. If it needs a field, you wanted an abstract class.
  • An enum is the correct singleton. enum Registry { INSTANCE; … } is serialisation-safe and reflection-proof, which the double-checked-locking singleton is not. Java Advanced revisits why.

Check yourself

1.class Cart implements Priced, Shippable, where both unrelated interfaces declare default String describe() and Cart does not override it. What happens?

D. Rule 3: two unrelated defaults with the same signature are a conflict the class must resolve, and the compiler refuses to guess. The override can pick one with Priced.super.describe(), combine both, or do something new.

A is a common guess but declaration order never affects resolution. B confuses this with dynamic dispatch, which picks among overrides in a class hierarchy, not among interface defaults. C describes what can happen when a class file is compiled against one version of an interface and run against another — a binary-compatibility problem, not a source one.

2.A team stores each product's category in the database as category.ordinal(). A year later someone adds ELECTRICAL between FASTENER and STRUCTURAL. What is the consequence?

B. An ordinal is nothing more than the source-order index. Shifting the constants shifts every number, and nothing fails loudly: the data simply reads back as the wrong category. Persist name() or a dedicated code field instead.

A is false — the ordinal is fixed at compile time from the declaration order. C: the array just got longer; index 1 is valid and returns the wrong constant. D: the compiler has no notion of an enum being "published" and allows any edit.

3.interface Audited { default String toString() { return "audited"; } } — does this compile, and why?

C. The language forbids it outright, and rule 1 explains why it would be pointless anyway: every class already inherits toString from Object, a class, and a class method always beats an interface default.

A would require interfaces to beat classes, which is backwards. B: toString is not final — you override it all the time. D is invented; default methods can return anything.

Section 4

Lambdas, functional interfaces and method references

A lambda is a compact way to write an object that implements a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method (§3). p -> p.onHand() < 5 is not a function floating free; it becomes an instance of whatever single-method interface the surrounding code expects, and that interface's method body is the lambda. Nothing else about it is new. What makes lambdas worth a whole section is how the compiler decides which interface, what the lambda may touch from its surroundings, and the four shorthand forms called method references that replace most lambdas you would otherwise write.

The mental model to carry through streams (§5) and collectors (§6): a lambda has no type of its own. The same text x -> x is a Function<String,String> in one place and a UnaryOperator<Integer> in another, and in a place with no target type at all it is a compile error.

The interfaces you will actually use

Almost every lambda in real code targets one of the interfaces in java.util.function. Learn these shapes and you can read any stream pipeline.

Core functional interfaces, their abstract method and a warehouse example
InterfaceMethodShapeExample
Function<T,R>R apply(T)one in, one outProduct::sku
BiFunction<T,U,R>R apply(T,U)two in, one out(sku, qty) -> new OrderLine(sku, qty)
Predicate<T>boolean test(T)one in, yes/nop -> p.onHand() == 0
Consumer<T>void accept(T)one in, nothing outSystem.out::println
Supplier<T>T get()nothing in, one outArrayList::new
UnaryOperator<T>T apply(T)Function where in = outString::trim
BinaryOperator<T>T apply(T,T)BiFunction with all three the sameInteger::sum
IntPredicate, IntFunction<R>, ToIntFunction<T>, IntBinaryOperator…as above, on intprimitive specialisationsmapToInt(Product::onHand) takes a ToIntFunction

The primitive variants exist because generics cannot take int (Fundamentals §13). Function<Product,Integer> would box every result; ToIntFunction<Product> does not. Streams use them everywhere — mapToInt, IntStream.sum() — and §5 shows why that matters.

Worked example

Every lambda and every kind of method reference, applied to stock levels. Read the comments on the right of each declaration first; they name which of the four reference forms it is.

javaLambdas.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.BiFunction;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Predicate;
import java.util.function.Supplier;
import java.util.function.UnaryOperator;
 
public class Lambdas {
 
    record Product(String sku, int priceInCents, int onHand) {}
 
    static boolean isLowStock(Product p) { return p.onHand() < 5; }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> stock = List.of(
                new Product("BOLT-7", 80, 500),
                new Product("GIRD-1", 120_000, 2),
                new Product("CAM-9", 425, 3));
 
        // a lambda has no type of its own: each one below is typed by its target
        Predicate<Product> low = p -> p.onHand() < 5;
        Function<Product, String> sku = Product::sku;                 // unbound instance method
        Supplier<List<Product>> fresh = ArrayList::new;               // constructor
        BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> max = Math::max;        // static method
        Product sample = stock.get(0);
        Supplier<String> boundSku = sample::sku;                      // bound instance method
 
        System.out.println("low stock:         " + stock.stream().filter(low).map(sku).toList());
        System.out.println("fresh list empty:  " + fresh.get().isEmpty());
        System.out.println("max:               " + max.apply(80, 4_250));
        System.out.println("bound receiver:    " + boundSku.get());
 
        // composition builds new functions from old ones without a class in sight
        Predicate<Product> cheap = p -> p.priceInCents() < 1_000;
        Predicate<Product> reorder = low.and(cheap.negate());
        System.out.println("low and not cheap: " + stock.stream().filter(reorder).map(Product::sku).toList());
 
        Function<Integer, Integer> addTax = cents -> cents + cents / 5;
        Function<Integer, Integer> addShipping = cents -> cents + 150;
        System.out.println("tax then shipping: " + addTax.andThen(addShipping).apply(1_000));
        System.out.println("shipping then tax: " + addTax.compose(addShipping).apply(1_000));
 
        // capture: the lambda copies the VALUE of threshold, so threshold must never change
        int threshold = 5;
        Predicate<Product> under = p -> p.onHand() < threshold;
        // threshold = 6;   // uncomment: "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final"
        System.out.println("under threshold:   " + stock.stream().filter(under).count());
 
        Comparator<Product> byPrice = Comparator.comparingInt(Product::priceInCents);
        List<Product> sorted = new ArrayList<>(stock);
        sorted.sort(byPrice.reversed());
        System.out.println("priciest first:    " + sorted.stream().map(Product::sku).toList());
        System.out.println("own static helper: " + stock.stream().filter(Lambdas::isLowStock).count());
 
        UnaryOperator<String> shout = String::toUpperCase;
        System.out.println(shout.apply("ready"));
    }
}
Expected output
low stock:         [GIRD-1, CAM-9]
fresh list empty:  true
max:               4250
bound receiver:    BOLT-7
low and not cheap: [GIRD-1]
tax then shipping: 1350
shipping then tax: 1380
under threshold:   2
priciest first:    [GIRD-1, CAM-9, BOLT-7]
own static helper: 2
READY

andThen and compose are the same two functions in opposite orders: f.andThen(g) runs f first, f.compose(g) runs g first. The 30-cent difference in the output is tax applied before or after the shipping charge — exactly the kind of thing a pricing bug is made of, so read these carefully in code review. Predicate.and, or and negate compose tests the same way.

Four kinds of method reference

A method reference is a lambda whose body is a single call that forwards its parameters unchanged. The compiler expands it; there is nothing a reference can do that a lambda cannot, and the reverse is also true. The four forms differ in where the receiver comes from.

Expand a method reference
Bound versus unbound is the one that bites

sample::sku and Product::sku look alike and differ completely. The first is bound: the receiver sample is evaluated once, when the reference is created, and the resulting Supplier takes no parameters. The second is unbound: the receiver arrives later as the first parameter, so it is a Function<Product,String>. System.out::println is bound to the System.out object that existed at that moment — reassign System.setOut afterwards and the reference still prints to the old stream.

Watch the compiler type a lambda

Target typing Simulated ← → to step
Source
Comparator<Product> byPrice = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.priceInCents(), b.priceInCents());
 
var byName = (a, b) -> a.name().compareTo(b.name());
 
Object o = p -> p.sku();
 
Function<Product, String> sku = p -> p.sku();
Supplier<String> hello = () -> "hello";
What the compiler knows
Diagnostic

What a lambda can touch

A lambda body can use the enclosing method's local variables, the enclosing instance's fields, and this. The rules for each are different, and the difference is the source of most lambda bugs.

A captured local must be effectively final: assigned exactly once and never changed, whether or not you wrote final. The reason is that the lambda copies the value when it is created. The lambda may outlive the method — be stored in a field, run on another thread — long after the method's stack frame is gone, so there is no variable left to share. Allowing writes would give you two copies that silently disagree, so the compiler forbids them on both sides.

If you need a mutable counter, the fix is not int[] count = {0} — that compiles because the reference is effectively final, but it is a thread-unsafe hack. Use a reduce or count() on the stream, or an AtomicInteger if you genuinely need shared mutable state.

Inside a lambda, this means the enclosing instance — the same object it meant on the line before the lambda. A lambda introduces no new scope for this, which is why this::isLowStock works in an instance method and why a lambda can read fields with no qualifier.

Inside an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object itself, and the enclosing instance is Outer.this. This is the single behavioural difference between a lambda and an anonymous class that implements the same interface, and it is why an IDE's "convert to lambda" can change meaning if the body uses this. §2 covered the anonymous-class side.

None of the java.util.function interfaces declare throws. So path -> Files.readString(path) does not compile as a Function: readString throws IOException, and apply is not allowed to. The error message — unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown — points at the lambda body.

Your options are to catch inside the lambda and wrap in an UncheckedIOException, to declare your own functional interface whose method does throws, or to move the I/O out of the pipeline entirely. Wrapping is the usual answer; silently swallowing the exception in a catch that returns null is the usual mistake.

Gotchas
  • Overloads plus lambdas confuse inference. submit(() -> doWork()) on an ExecutorService has both a Runnable and a Callable overload. If doWork returns a value the Callable wins; if not, Runnable. Change the method's return type and you silently change which overload is called.
  • @FunctionalInterface is a promise, not a requirement. Any single-abstract-method interface works as a lambda target. The annotation makes the compiler reject a second abstract method, which protects callers who rely on lambdas. Put it on every interface you intend to be used that way.
  • A lambda is not always a new object. A non-capturing lambda is typically allocated once and reused; a capturing one is allocated per evaluation. Do not compare lambdas with == or use them as map keys.
  • Long lambdas are a smell. A body of more than a few lines belongs in a named method, referenced with this::name. The name documents it, and a stack trace through lambda$main$3 tells you nothing.

Check yourself

1.Inside a method: int shipped = 0; orders.forEach(o -> shipped += o.qty()); — what happens?

C. A lambda captures a copy of the local's value, so a write inside the body could never reach the variable outside. Rather than let that silently happen, the language refuses to compile any lambda that assigns to a captured local — or any method that assigns to a local a lambda has captured.

B is what would happen if the rule did not exist, and is exactly the surprise the rule prevents. A requires shared variables, which Java lambdas do not have. D is about modifying a collection during iteration, which this code does not do. Use orders.stream().mapToInt(Order::qty).sum().

2.Comparator<String> c = String::compareToIgnoreCase; — which kind of method reference is this, and what does it expand to?

B. compareToIgnoreCase is an instance method, and String:: names the type rather than an object, so the reference is unbound: the first parameter of the target method becomes the receiver and the rest become arguments. Two parameters in, one receiver plus one argument out — the arities line up.

A would need a static method, and there is none with that name. C would need an expression before the ::, not a type. D is the trap: the counts do match once you account for the receiver, which is the whole point of the unbound form.

3.Which of these can the lambda (a, b) -> a + b be assigned to without error? Select all that apply.

A and D. Both targets have a two-parameter abstract method, and + works on the inferred types — numeric addition for Integer, concatenation for String. The same lambda text means two different things depending on the target, which is the lesson of this section.

B fails because Function.apply takes one argument and the lambda declares two. C fails because var infers from the initialiser and a lambda has no intrinsic type to infer.

Section 5

Streams: pipelines and laziness

A stream is not a collection. It holds no elements; it is a description of a computation over a source — a List, an array, a range of numbers, lines of a file — expressed as a chain of operations. Nothing happens when you build the chain. The work starts only when a terminal operation asks for a result, and then elements flow through the whole chain one at a time, each operation pulling from the one before it. That single fact — vertical, element-by-element, on demand — explains every behaviour in this section, including the ones that look like magic and the ones that look like bugs.

The vocabulary: a source (stock.stream()), zero or more intermediate operations that return a new stream (filter, map, sorted, limit…), and exactly one terminal operation that produces a value or a side effect and consumes the stream (toList, count, findFirst, forEach…).

Worked example: proving laziness

The println calls inside the lambdas are there only to make the order of execution visible. Read the trace against the pipeline that produced it.

javaStreamLazy.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
 
public class StreamLazy {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> skus = List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "GIRD-1", "CAM-9");
 
        System.out.println("-- no terminal operation: nothing runs --");
        skus.stream()
            .filter(s -> { System.out.println("  filter " + s); return !s.startsWith("B"); })
            .map(s -> { System.out.println("  map    " + s); return s.toLowerCase(); });
        System.out.println("(pipeline built, zero elements processed)");
 
        System.out.println("-- findFirst: one element at a time, and it stops early --");
        Optional<String> first = skus.stream()
            .filter(s -> { System.out.println("  filter " + s); return !s.startsWith("B"); })
            .map(s -> { System.out.println("  map    " + s); return s.toLowerCase(); })
            .findFirst();
        System.out.println("result: " + first.orElse("none"));
 
        System.out.println("-- sorted is a barrier: every element arrives before any leaves --");
        List<String> out = skus.stream()
            .filter(s -> { System.out.println("  filter " + s); return !s.startsWith("N"); })
            .sorted()
            .map(s -> { System.out.println("  map    " + s); return s.toLowerCase(); })
            .limit(2)
            .toList();
        System.out.println("result: " + out);
    }
}
Expected output
-- no terminal operation: nothing runs --
(pipeline built, zero elements processed)
-- findFirst: one element at a time, and it stops early --
  filter BOLT-7
  filter NUT-3
  map    NUT-3
result: nut-3
-- sorted is a barrier: every element arrives before any leaves --
  filter BOLT-7
  filter NUT-3
  filter GIRD-1
  filter CAM-9
  map    BOLT-7
  map    CAM-9
result: [bolt-7, cam-9]

Three lessons, one per block:

  • No terminal, no work. The first pipeline has filter and map but nothing printed. A stream you forget to terminate is a no-op, not an error — and a common bug.
  • Elements flow vertically, not in stages. BOLT-7 went through filter and was rejected before NUT-3 was even looked at. NUT-3 passed, was mapped, and reached findFirst, which had what it needed and stopped. GIRD-1 and CAM-9 were never touched. That is short-circuiting.
  • Stateful operations break the flow. sorted cannot emit its first element until it has seen its last — the smallest might be at the end. So every element is filtered first, then the sorted ones start moving: BOLT-7, CAM-9 are mapped, and limit(2) stops the third before map ever sees it.

Watch the pull

One element at a time Simulated ← → to step
Source
List<String> skus = List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "GIRD-1", "CAM-9");
Optional<String> first = skus.stream()
    .filter(s -> !s.startsWith("B"))
    .map(String::toLowerCase)
    .findFirst();

Worked example: a real report

The laziness demonstration above is contrived. This is what stream code looks like in practice — a stock-value report, with the seven operations you will use most, each commented with the rule it illustrates.

javaStreamPipeline.java
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;
 
public class StreamPipeline {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, TOOLING }
    record Product(String sku, Category category, int priceInCents, int onHand) {
        int stockValueInCents() { return priceInCents * onHand; }
    }
    record OrderLine(String sku, int qty) {}
    record Order(String id, List<OrderLine> lines) {}
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> stock = List.of(
            new Product("BOLT-7", Category.FASTENER,   80,      500),
            new Product("NUT-3",  Category.FASTENER,   25,      2_000),
            new Product("GIRD-1", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000, 2),
            new Product("ROD-4",  Category.STRUCTURAL, 9_500,   12),
            new Product("CAM-9",  Category.TOOLING,    4_250,   3));
 
        // 1. filter -> sorted -> limit -> map -> collect: the three most valuable non-tooling lines
        List<String> report = stock.stream()
            .filter(p -> p.category() != Category.TOOLING)
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Product::stockValueInCents).reversed())
            .limit(3)
            .map(p -> p.sku() + "=" + p.stockValueInCents() / 100 + ".00")
            .toList();
        System.out.println("top value:     " + report);
 
        // 2. primitive streams: no boxing, statistics built in
        int totalUnits = stock.stream().mapToInt(Product::onHand).sum();
        double avgPrice = stock.stream().mapToInt(Product::priceInCents).average().orElse(0);
        System.out.printf("units=%d avgPrice=%.1f%n", totalUnits, avgPrice);
 
        // 3. flatMap: an order has many lines; flatten them before counting
        List<Order> orders = List.of(
            new Order("A1", List.of(new OrderLine("BOLT-7", 40), new OrderLine("NUT-3", 100))),
            new Order("A2", List.of(new OrderLine("BOLT-7", 10))),
            new Order("A3", List.of()));
        int boltsOrdered = orders.stream()
            .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
            .filter(l -> l.sku().equals("BOLT-7"))
            .mapToInt(OrderLine::qty)
            .sum();
        System.out.println("bolts ordered: " + boltsOrdered);
 
        // 4. reduce: the identity must be neutral for the operation (0 is right for max of lengths, wrong for min)
        int longestSku = stock.stream().map(Product::sku).mapToInt(String::length).reduce(0, Math::max);
        System.out.println("longest sku:   " + longestSku);
 
        // 5. anyMatch short-circuits; distinct is stateful (it remembers what it has seen)
        boolean anyEmpty = orders.stream().anyMatch(o -> o.lines().isEmpty());
        long categories = stock.stream().map(Product::category).distinct().count();
        System.out.println("empty order:   " + anyEmpty + ", distinct categories: " + categories);
 
        // 6. a range as a source
        String bins = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4).mapToObj(i -> "BIN-" + i).reduce((a, b) -> a + "," + b).orElse("");
        System.out.println("bins:          " + bins);
 
        // 7. a stream is single-use
        var once = stock.stream();
        once.count();
        try { once.count(); }
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("second use:    " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
Expected output
top value:     [GIRD-1=2400.00, ROD-4=1140.00, NUT-3=500.00]
units=2517 avgPrice=26771.0
bolts ordered: 50
longest sku:   6
empty order:   true, distinct categories: 3
bins:          BIN-1,BIN-2,BIN-3,BIN-4
second use:    stream has already been operated upon or closed

Two of those deserve a closer look. flatMap takes a function that returns a stream per element and splices all those streams into one — the only way to get from a list of orders to a flat sequence of their lines. reduce folds the elements with a binary operator; the two-argument form needs an identity that leaves any value unchanged (0 for sum or max-of-non-negatives, 1 for product, "" for concatenation), and the one-argument form returns an Optional because an empty stream has nothing to fold. Pass a non-neutral identity and the result is quietly wrong, which is why block 6 uses the Optional form rather than reduce("", …) and a leading comma.

Build the pipeline

The report wanted is the SKUs of the three alphabetically-first products that are in stock. Put the six operations in the only order that type-checks and gives the right answer.

  1. 1 .sorted()
  2. 2 List<String> skus = stock.stream()
  3. 3 .toList();
  4. 4 .map(Product::sku)
  5. 5 .limit(3)
  6. 6 .filter(p -> p.onHand() > 0)

Correct. filter must come before map because it reads onHand(), which only a Product has; after map the elements are Strings. sorted() with no comparator needs Comparable elements — String is, Product is not, so it must follow map. limit(3) after sorted gives the three smallest; before it, you would sort whichever three happened to come first. And sorted is a barrier: it drains everything upstream before limit can short-circuit anything, so put filter ahead of it to give it less to drain.

Stateless, stateful, short-circuiting

Stream operations by category
CategoryOperationsBehaviour
Stateless intermediatefilter, map, mapToInt, flatMap, peekEach element handled alone; can stream forever; cheap.
Stateful intermediatesorted, distinctsorted buffers everything; distinct keeps a set of what it has seen. Both are barriers to laziness and both need memory proportional to the input.
Short-circuiting intermediatelimit, takeWhileCan finish an infinite stream. limit after a stateful op still has to wait for it.
Short-circuiting terminalfindFirst, findAny, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatchStop pulling as soon as the answer is known.
Full terminaltoList, collect, count, sum, reduce, forEach, maxConsume every element.
Gotchas
  • A stream is single-use. Once a terminal operation has run, the stream is spent; a second one throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Store the collection and call stream() again.
  • Side effects in map and filter are a smell. A lambda that writes to a list outside the pipeline works until someone adds parallel(), and then it corrupts the list. Collect results with the terminal operation; use peek only for debugging.
  • map boxes, mapToInt does not. stock.stream().map(Product::onHand).reduce(0, Integer::sum) allocates an Integer per element and unboxes it again; mapToInt(Product::onHand).sum() works on int throughout. For numeric work, go primitive at the earliest opportunity.
  • parallel() is not a free speed-up. It splits the source across the common fork-join pool, which pays off for large, splittable sources with CPU-heavy, side-effect-free operations — and costs more than it gains for small lists, I/O, or anything with a synchronized inside. Measure before and after; never add it by reflex. Java Advanced covers the machinery.
  • Encounter order is not guaranteed everywhere. forEach on a parallel stream runs in whatever order threads arrive; forEachOrdered preserves it. findAny may return something other than the first.

Check yourself

1.skus.stream().map(s -> { System.out.println(s); return s.trim(); }).filter(s -> !s.isEmpty()); — with four non-empty SKUs in the list, how many lines are printed?

D. There is no terminal operation. map and filter are intermediate; they build a pipeline and return it, and nobody ever asks the pipeline for an element. The lambdas are never invoked.

A is what you get after appending .toList() or .count(). B misunderstands the chain: each element passes through map once, whatever comes after. C: map never short-circuits; only operations like findFirst and limit do.

2.Prices are [90, 10, 50, 20]. What do prices.stream().sorted().limit(2).toList() and prices.stream().limit(2).sorted().toList() return?

B. Order of operations is the order of the pipeline. The first sorts all four, then keeps the two smallest. The second keeps the first two in encounter order — 90, 10 — and then sorts those, giving [10, 90].

A is the intuition that stream operations are declarative set operations; they are not, they are sequential stages. C forgets that sorted still runs in the second pipeline, just on fewer elements. D: sorted is happy with any finite stream, including one limit truncated.

3.Stream<Product> s = stock.stream(); long n = s.count(); List<Product> all = s.toList(); — what happens on the third statement?

C. A terminal operation closes the pipeline; the stream object records that it has been operated upon and rejects any further use with IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Create a fresh stream from the collection for each query.

A describes a collection, not a stream — the source is reusable, the pipeline is not. B is how an exhausted Iterator behaves, and streams chose to fail loudly instead. D: the compiler has no notion of single-use variables; this is purely a runtime check.

Section 6

Collectors and grouping

A terminal operation has to put the elements somewhere. collect is the general-purpose one, and a Collector is its recipe: how to create a container, how to add one element to it, how to merge two containers (for parallel streams), and how to finish. You will almost never write one — the Collectors class ships every recipe a report needs, and they compose: a groupingBy takes a downstream collector that decides what happens to the elements inside each group.

That composition is the whole skill. Once you can read groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream) as "bucket by this, into that kind of map, then do this to each bucket", every report in the warehouse is a one-liner, and you stop writing the nested-loop-and-temporary-map code that §11 of Fundamentals was full of.

Worked example

Seven collectors against the stock list. Every line of the output below was produced by running this program during the build.

javaGrouping.java
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
 
public class Grouping {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    record Product(String sku, Category category, int priceInCents, int onHand) {
        long stockValueInCents() { return (long) priceInCents * onHand; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> stock = List.of(
            new Product("BOLT-7", Category.FASTENER,        80,  400),
            new Product("NUT-3",  Category.FASTENER,        25, 1200),
            new Product("PIN-2",  Category.FASTENER,        15,    6),
            new Product("GIRD-1", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000,    3),
            new Product("ROD-4",  Category.STRUCTURAL,   4_500,   40),
            new Product("CAM-9",  Category.MOTION,       2_300,    2));
 
        // 1. groupingBy with a map factory and a downstream: stock value per category
        Map<Category, Long> valueByCategory = stock.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Product::category, TreeMap::new,
                     Collectors.summingLong(Product::stockValueInCents)));
        System.out.println("value by category = " + valueByCategory);
 
        // 2. partitioningBy: always exactly two keys, even when one side is empty
        Map<Boolean, List<String>> lowStock = stock.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(p -> p.onHand() < 10,
                     Collectors.mapping(Product::sku, Collectors.toList())));
        System.out.println("low stock         = " + lowStock.get(true));
        System.out.println("healthy           = " + lowStock.get(false));
 
        // 3. collectingAndThen unwraps the Optional that maxBy produces
        Map<Category, String> priciest = stock.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Product::category, TreeMap::new,
                     Collectors.collectingAndThen(
                         Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Product::priceInCents)),
                         opt -> opt.map(Product::sku).orElse("-"))));
        System.out.println("priciest per cat  = " + priciest);
 
        // 4. joining with a separator, prefix and suffix
        String skus = stock.stream().map(Product::sku).sorted()
            .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));
        System.out.println("all skus          = " + skus);
 
        // 5. toMap with a merge function: three FASTENER prices collide on one key
        Map<Category, Integer> cheapest = stock.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::category, Product::priceInCents,
                     Math::min, TreeMap::new));
        System.out.println("cheapest per cat  = " + cheapest);
 
        // 6. teeing: two collectors over one pass, merged into one result
        String summary = stock.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.teeing(
                Collectors.counting(),
                Collectors.summingLong(Product::stockValueInCents),
                (count, total) -> count + " products worth " + total + "c"));
        System.out.println("summary           = " + summary);
 
        // 7. toMap WITHOUT a merge function throws on the first duplicate key
        try {
            stock.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Product::category, Product::sku));
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("no merge fn       = " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Expected output
value by category = {FASTENER=62090, STRUCTURAL=540000, MOTION=4600}
low stock         = [PIN-2, GIRD-1, CAM-9]
healthy           = [BOLT-7, NUT-3, ROD-4]
priciest per cat  = {FASTENER=BOLT-7, STRUCTURAL=GIRD-1, MOTION=CAM-9}
all skus          = [BOLT-7, CAM-9, GIRD-1, NUT-3, PIN-2, ROD-4]
cheapest per cat  = {FASTENER=15, STRUCTURAL=4500, MOTION=2300}
summary           = 6 products worth 606690c
no merge fn       = Duplicate key FASTENER (attempted merging values BOLT-7 and NUT-3)

Three things to notice. The highlighted groupingBy has three arguments — classifier, map factory, downstream — and the two-argument form groupingBy(classifier, downstream) is the same thing with a HashMap, which is why the output would be in an unspecified order without TreeMap::new. maxBy returns an Optional because a collector cannot know its group will be non-empty, so collectingAndThen exists to apply one last function to the finished container. And the final line is the error you get from the two-argument toMap: it does not pick a winner, it refuses — the merge function in step 5 is what tells it how.

The catalogue

Collectors that build a collection
CollectorProducesWorth knowing
toList()a mutable List (in practice an ArrayList, but not guaranteed)Since Java 16 prefer stream.toList(), which returns an unmodifiable list and reads better.
toUnmodifiableList() / toUnmodifiableSet()an immutable collectionThrows NullPointerException if any element is null, like List.of.
toSet()a HashSet, order unspecifiedUse toCollection(TreeSet::new) or LinkedHashSet::new when order matters.
toCollection(supplier)whatever you constructThe escape hatch for any Collection type.
toMap(keyFn, valueFn)a HashMapThrows IllegalStateException on a duplicate key. Also throws NullPointerException on a null value, unlike HashMap.put.
