toMap(keyFn, valueFn, mergeFn)a HashMapThe merge function receives the existing and the new value for a colliding key and returns the one to keep: Math::min, (a, b) -> a, Integer::sum.
toMap(keyFn, valueFn, mergeFn, mapSupplier)whatever map you constructTreeMap::new for sorted keys, LinkedHashMap::new to keep encounter order, () -> new EnumMap<>(Category.class) for enum keys.
Collectors that reduce to one value
CollectorProducesWorth knowing
counting()LongAlways Long, never Integer — a frequent compile error inside groupingBy.
summingInt / summingLong / summingDouble(fn)Integer / Long / DoublePick the width before the overflow, not after: stock value in cents times quantity needs summingLong.
averagingInt / Long / Double(fn)DoubleReturns 0.0 for an empty group, which is indistinguishable from a real zero average.
summarizingInt / Long / Double(fn)IntSummaryStatistics etc.Count, sum, min, average and max in one pass. The right answer when you need more than one of them.
minBy / maxBy(comparator)Optional<T>Optional because a collector cannot promise the group is non-empty. Unwrap with collectingAndThen.
joining(), joining(sep), joining(sep, prefix, suffix)StringOnly accepts a Stream<CharSequence> — map(Object::toString) or map(Product::sku) first.
reducing(identity, mapper, op)whatever op returnsA general fold as a collector, so it can sit downstream of groupingBy. For a bare stream, reduce is clearer.
teeing(c1, c2, merger)whatever merger returnsJava 12+. Runs two collectors over the same elements in one pass and combines their results — count and sum, min and max.
Grouping collectors
CollectorProducesWorth knowing
groupingBy(classifier)Map<K, List<T>> in a HashMapShorthand for groupingBy(classifier, toList()). Keys only appear for values that occurred.
groupingBy(classifier, downstream)Map<K, D> in a HashMapThe one you want most of the time. D is whatever the downstream produces.
groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream)Map<K, D> in the map you constructNote the argument order: factory in the middle, unlike toMap where it is last.
partitioningBy(predicate)Map<Boolean, List<T>>Always has both keys. groupingBy(p -> p.onHand() < 10) would omit true when nothing is low — then get(true) returns null.
partitioningBy(predicate, downstream)Map<Boolean, D>Same composition rule as groupingBy.

These wrap another collector and change what it sees or what it returns. They are pointless on a bare stream — map and filter do that — and essential inside a group, where there is no stream to call map on.

Downstream adapter collectors
CollectorDoesStream equivalent, if it were a stream
mapping(fn, downstream)transforms each element before the downstream sees it.map(fn)
filtering(pred, downstream)drops elements the downstream never sees — but the group key still appears, possibly with an empty result.filter(pred), except the key survives
flatMapping(fn, downstream)explodes each element into a stream of elements for the downstream.flatMap(fn)
collectingAndThen(downstream, finisher)applies one function to the downstream's final resultthere is none — this is the only way to post-process a group's value

That filtering subtlety is the common one: groupingBy(Product::category, filtering(p -> p.onHand() < 10, toList())) gives you every category, some mapped to an empty list. filter(…) before the collect gives you only the categories that have a low-stock item. Both are correct; they answer different questions.

Build a grouping

Six products, three choices. The expression updates as you change them, and the map below it is what that expression would produce — including the order you would see when you print it.

groupingBy, assembled

Match the need to the collector

Drag a collector onto its slot, or click one then click the other

Each report line below has exactly one collector that produces it directly.

All four. partitioningBy is the only grouping that guarantees both keys. teeing is the only way to run two collectors over one pass. toMap with a merge function is the idiom for "sum into a map by key"; without Integer::sum the second line for a SKU would throw. And summarizingInt is one pass for all four statistics, where counting plus averagingInt plus minBy plus maxBy would be four.

When a loop is clearer

Collectors earn their place when the shape of the result is a standard one — a map of groups, a joined string, a summary. They stop earning it when you find yourself nesting three downstreams deep to express a rule that is two if statements in a loop, or when the "collector" needs to update two unrelated structures at once. The test is whether a colleague can read the result type and know what it contains: Map<Category, Map<Boolean, Long>> is still readable; Map<Category, Map<Boolean, Map<String, Optional<Product>>>> is a sign to write a small record and a plain loop.

Collector gotchas
  • toMap throws on duplicates and on null values. The duplicate rule is deliberate — silently keeping one would hide a data problem — but it surprises everyone once. The null value rule differs from HashMap.put, which accepts null; use Optional or a sentinel, or fall back to a loop.
  • counting() returns Long. Map<Category, Integer> n = … groupingBy(…, counting()) does not compile. Declare Long, or use summingInt(p -> 1) if you genuinely need an Integer.
  • groupingBy rejects null keys. A classifier that returns null — a product with no category — throws NullPointerException mid-collection. Map it to a sentinel first, or filter it out and report it separately.
  • The map you get back is mutable but unspecified. groupingBy and toMap promise a Map, not a HashMap; do not cast, and do not rely on its iteration order unless you supplied the factory.
  • Collectors.toList() is not Stream.toList(). The collector gives a list you may modify (today it is an ArrayList; the Javadoc does not promise it). The Java 16 stream method gives an unmodifiable list. Code that adds to the result after collecting works with one and throws UnsupportedOperationException with the other.

Check yourself

1.No product has zero stock. What does stock.stream().collect(groupingBy(p -> p.onHand() == 0)).get(true) return, and what does the same with partitioningBy return?

C. groupingBy only creates a key when an element maps to it, so with no out-of-stock products the key true never exists and Map.get returns null. partitioningBy is specified to always contain both true and false, so the answer is an empty list — safe to iterate without a null check.

A and B assume the two behave alike; the difference is the entire reason partitioningBy exists. D is wrong because Map.get never throws for a missing key — that is what makes the null dangerous.

2.You want the total onHand per SKU. The stream contains two lines for BOLT-7. Which call is correct?

B. The merge function receives the value already in the map and the new value for the same key, and Integer::sum adds them. groupingBy(Product::sku, summingInt(Product::onHand)) would also be correct and is arguably clearer.

A throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key BOLT-7 the moment the second line arrives. C counts lines per SKU, not quantity — it would say 2 for BOLT-7 regardless of stock. D compiles and runs, but keeps only the last value for each SKU, silently discarding the first line's quantity.

3.Which of these statements about groupingBy(Product::category, filtering(p -> p.onHand() < 10, toList())) are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. The classifier runs on every element, so every category becomes a key; the downstream filtering then decides what goes into each bucket, which can be nothing.

B is the trap: filtering before the collect removes whole categories whose products are all healthy, so those keys never appear. C is wrong because the two-argument groupingBy uses a HashMap; you would need the three-argument form with TreeMap::new.

Section 7

Optional

Fundamentals §11 diagnosed the NullPointerException and §L's findById returned null for a miss, with a note that the modern alternative was coming. This is it. Optional<T> is a container that holds either one value or nothing, and its only real purpose is to make a return type say "this may be absent" so loudly that the caller cannot forget. A method returning Product might return null and you have to read the Javadoc to know. A method returning Optional<Product> has told you, in the signature, and the compiler will not let you treat the result as a Product without deciding what to do about the empty case.

That decision is the whole API. Every method on Optional is a different way of answering "and if it is empty?" — substitute a value, substitute another lookup, throw, do nothing, or carry the emptiness forward through a chain so the question is answered once, at the end.

Worked example

javaOptionals.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
 
public class Optionals {
 
    record Product(String sku, int priceInCents, String supplierSku) { }   // supplierSku may be null
 
    static final Map<String, Product> CATALOGUE = Map.of(
        "BOLT-7", new Product("BOLT-7", 80, "ACME-0071"),
        "NUT-3",  new Product("NUT-3", 25, null),
        "FREE-1", new Product("FREE-1", 0, "ACME-0999"));
 
    // The return type says it: a lookup may find nothing.
    static Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(CATALOGUE.get(sku));
    }
 
    static Optional<String> supplierOf(Product p) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(p.supplierSku());
    }
 
    static int fallbackPrice() {
        System.out.println("  (fallbackPrice() was called)");
        return 999;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // map transforms the content when present; an empty Optional just flows through
        int bolt = findBySku("BOLT-7").map(Product::priceInCents).orElse(-1);
        int nope = findBySku("NOPE").map(Product::priceInCents).orElse(-1);
        System.out.println("BOLT-7 price = " + bolt + ", NOPE price = " + nope);
 
        // flatMap for a step that itself returns an Optional (no Optional<Optional<String>>)
        String s1 = findBySku("BOLT-7").flatMap(Optionals::supplierOf).orElse("no supplier");
        String s2 = findBySku("NUT-3").flatMap(Optionals::supplierOf).orElse("no supplier");
        System.out.println("suppliers    = " + s1 + " / " + s2);
 
        // filter turns a present value that fails the test into empty
        String priced = findBySku("FREE-1").filter(p -> p.priceInCents() > 0)
                                           .map(Product::sku).orElse("not priced");
        System.out.println("FREE-1       = " + priced);
 
        // orElse evaluates its argument ALWAYS; orElseGet only when empty
        System.out.println("orElse on a present value:");
        int a = findBySku("BOLT-7").map(Product::priceInCents).orElse(fallbackPrice());
        System.out.println("orElseGet on a present value:");
        int b = findBySku("BOLT-7").map(Product::priceInCents).orElseGet(Optionals::fallbackPrice);
        System.out.println("both gave " + a + " and " + b);
 
        // or() supplies an alternative Optional; orElseThrow names the failure
        Product p = findBySku("NOPE").or(() -> findBySku("NUT-3"))
                                     .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no product"));
        System.out.println("fallback     = " + p.sku());
 
        // ifPresentOrElse replaces the isPresent()/get() pair
        findBySku("CAM-9").ifPresentOrElse(
            x -> System.out.println("found " + x.sku()),
            () -> System.out.println("CAM-9 is not in the catalogue"));
 
        // Optional.stream(): keep only the hits, no isPresent() filter needed
        List<String> found = List.of("BOLT-7", "NOPE", "NUT-3").stream()
            .flatMap(sku -> findBySku(sku).stream())
            .map(Product::sku)
            .toList();
        System.out.println("found        = " + found);
 
        // of() refuses null; ofNullable() is the one that maps null to empty
        try {
            Optional.of(CATALOGUE.get("NOPE"));
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("Optional.of(null) threw NullPointerException");
        }
    }
}
Expected output
BOLT-7 price = 80, NOPE price = -1
suppliers    = ACME-0071 / no supplier
FREE-1       = not priced
orElse on a present value:
  (fallbackPrice() was called)
orElseGet on a present value:
both gave 80 and 80
fallback     = NUT-3
CAM-9 is not in the catalogue
found        = [BOLT-7, NUT-3]
Optional.of(null) threw NullPointerException

The line marked in red is the one people get wrong in production. orElse(fallbackPrice()) is an ordinary method call: Java evaluates the argument before calling orElse, whether or not the Optional is empty — so fallbackPrice() ran and printed its trace even though BOLT-7 was found. orElseGet takes a Supplier, and only invokes it when needed. For a constant, orElse is fine and reads better; for anything that does work — a database query, a default built from a file, logging — it must be orElseGet.

Watch a chain evaluate

The same four-step chain run three times: once for a product that exists, once for a SKU that does not, and once for a product that exists but fails the filter. Watch what the Optional contains after each stage.

Empty flows through Simulated ← → to step
Source
Optional<Product> found = findBySku(sku);
 
int price = found
    .map(Product::priceInCents)
    .filter(p -> p > 0)
    .orElse(0);
 
System.out.println(sku + " -> " + price);
State
Standard output

The API, by the question it answers

Optional methods grouped by purpose
QuestionMethodNotes
How do I make one?Optional.of(value)Throws NullPointerException on null — use it when null would be a bug.
Optional.ofNullable(value)Maps null to empty. The bridge from Map.get, legacy APIs and nullable fields.
Optional.empty()A shared singleton; == on empties is true but do not rely on it.
How do I transform the content?map(fn)Applies fn when present; a null result from fn becomes empty.
flatMap(fn)For an fn that itself returns Optional; avoids Optional<Optional<T>>.
filter(predicate)Present and passes → unchanged; present and fails → empty.
And if it is empty?orElse(value)Argument is evaluated eagerly. Fine for constants.
orElseGet(supplier)Supplier runs only when empty. Use for anything that costs.
orElseThrow() / orElseThrow(supplier)The no-argument form throws NoSuchElementException; the supplier form lets you name the failure. Prefer this over get(), which does the same thing with a misleading name.
or(supplier)Supplies another Optional: "try this lookup, then that one". Java 9+.
ifPresent(consumer) / ifPresentOrElse(consumer, runnable)Side-effect forms. Replace the if (o.isPresent()) o.get() pair.
How do I get out of it?stream()Zero or one element. Inside flatMap it drops the empties for free. Java 9+.
isPresent() / isEmpty()Legitimate in a condition that does something other than unwrap. A sign of trouble right before get().

OptionalInt, OptionalLong and OptionalDouble are what the primitive streams return from max(), average() and findFirst(). They avoid boxing, and have the same methods with primitive names — getAsInt, orElse(int) — but no map or filter. Convert with stream().boxed() if you need the full API.

Where Optional must not go

Its designers were explicit: Optional is for return types. Everywhere else it adds an allocation, a level of indirection and a second way to be empty (the Optional reference itself can still be null) without adding information.

Places Optional does not belong and what to use instead
Do not writeWhyInstead
A field: private Optional<String> supplier;It is not Serializable, it doubles the memory of every nullable field, and the field can still be null.A nullable field with an accessor that returns Optional: Optional<String> supplier() { return Optional.ofNullable(supplier); }
A parameter: void price(Optional<Discount> d)Every caller must wrap, and the method still has to handle a null argument.Two overloads, or a nullable parameter documented as such.
Optional<List<Product>>An empty list already means "none". Two ways to say nothing means two checks.Return the empty list.
As a collection element or map valueMap.get then returns null for a missing key and Optional.empty for a present-but-empty one — a distinction nobody wants.Store the value or nothing; Map.get and Optional.ofNullable at the read site.
Optional.of(x).map(…).orElse(…) on a value you know is presentIt is a verbose ternary.x == null ? d : f(x), or just f(x).
Optional gotchas
  • get() is orElseThrow() with a friendly name. It throws NoSuchElementException on empty, so findBySku(s).get() is a NullPointerException with a different class. If you must unwrap unconditionally, write orElseThrow() so the intent is visible.
  • isPresent() then get() is a null check in costume. It is exactly if (x != null) use(x) with more characters. The chain methods exist so that you never write it.
  • orElse(expensive()) always runs expensive(). Shown above. A logging statement inside the default method is the usual way this is discovered.
  • Returning null from a method typed Optional is the worst of both worlds. The caller trusted the signature and will call .map on null. Return Optional.empty(), always.
  • Optional is a value-based class. Do not synchronise on it, compare it with ==, or use it as a map key. Equality is by content: Optional.of(1).equals(Optional.of(1)) is true.

Check yourself

1.loadDefault() reads a configuration file and prints "loading" when it runs. What does findBySku("BOLT-7").map(Product::priceInCents).orElse(loadDefault()) print when BOLT-7 exists?

C. orElse is a normal method, and Java evaluates every argument before entering a method. The file is read, "loading" is printed, and then the value is thrown away because the Optional was present. orElseGet(Optionals::loadDefault) is the fix.

A is what people expect, and is exactly the behaviour of orElseGet, not orElse. B is backwards: orElseGet takes the Supplier; orElse takes a plain value, which is why it is eager. D is wrong because map never sees loadDefault at all.

2.supplierOf returns Optional<String>. What is the type of findBySku("NUT-3").map(Optionals::supplierOf)?

B. map wraps whatever the function returns, and the function returns an Optional, so you get an Optional inside an Optional. It compiles, and then .orElse("none") fails to compile because the outer content is not a String. flatMap is defined for exactly this: its function must return an Optional, and that Optional is used as the result directly.

A describes flatMap. C is wrong because map accepts any function; it has no idea Optional is special. D is wrong because no Optional method silently unwraps — that is the entire design.

3.Which uses of Optional are considered correct by its own designers? Select all that apply.

A and C. A return type is the intended use, and Optional.stream() was added in Java 9 precisely so that a lookup returning Optional composes with flatMap to drop the misses.

B fails twice: Optional is not Serializable, so the entity will not serialise, and the field itself can still be null. D forces every caller to wrap — price(p, Optional.empty()) — and the method must still guard against a null argument; an overload price(Product) is the idiom.

Section 8

Records

Fundamentals §10 ended with the observation that equals, hashCode and toString are forty lines of ceremony you get wrong once per career, and that a record gives you all three for free. Here is the full story. A record is a class whose entire state is declared in its header, and from that header the compiler derives everything a value type needs: a private final field per component, a canonical constructor that takes them all, an accessor per component, and equals, hashCode and toString that use every component. What you give up is exactly the freedom that made the hand-written versions error-prone: no extra instance fields, no setters, no superclass, no subclasses.

The design intent is the phrase "a transparent carrier for immutable data". OrderLine is one: three values, no identity beyond them, equal when the values are equal. InventoryService is not: it has behaviour, mutable state and a lifecycle. Knowing which of your classes are records and which are not is most of the skill.

Worked example

javaRecords.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
public class Records {
 
    record OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) {
        // compact constructor: no parameter list; runs BEFORE the fields are assigned
        OrderLine {
            if (sku == null || sku.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku required");
            if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty);
            sku = sku.strip().toUpperCase();          // reassigns the PARAMETER; the field is set from it after
        }
        int totalInCents() { return qty * unitPriceInCents; }
    }
 
    record Address(String city, String country) { }
 
    record Order(long id, Address shipTo, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        Order {
            lines = List.copyOf(lines);               // defensive, immutable copy
        }
        static Order of(long id, Address shipTo, OrderLine... lines) {   // static factory
            return new Order(id, shipTo, List.of(lines));
        }
        int totalInCents() { return lines.stream().mapToInt(OrderLine::totalInCents).sum(); }
    }
 
    record Bag(List<String> items) { }                // NO defensive copy: deliberately leaky
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderLine a = new OrderLine("  bolt-7 ", 10, 80);
        OrderLine b = new OrderLine("BOLT-7", 10, 80);
        System.out.println("toString  = " + a);
        System.out.println("equals    = " + a.equals(b) + ", same hash = " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()));
        System.out.println("accessor  = " + a.sku() + " x" + a.qty());
 
        try { new OrderLine("NUT-3", 0, 25); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected  = " + e.getMessage()); }
 
        OrderLine nut = new OrderLine("NUT-3", 4, 25);
        List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of(a, nut));
        Order order = Order.of(1001L, new Address("Leeds", "UK"), a, nut);
        Order copied = new Order(1001L, new Address("Leeds", "UK"), lines);
        lines.add(new OrderLine("CAM-9", 1, 2_300));  // the caller mutates its own list afterwards
        System.out.println("totals    = " + order.totalInCents() + "c and " + copied.totalInCents() + "c (the copy did not change)");
        System.out.println("nested eq = " + order.equals(copied));
 
        Map<OrderLine, Integer> picked = new HashMap<>();
        picked.merge(a, 1, Integer::sum);
        picked.merge(b, 1, Integer::sum);               // an equal record is the same key
        System.out.println("map keys  = " + picked.size() + ", picks of BOLT-7 = " + picked.get(b));
 
        // shallow immutability: the reference cannot change, the list behind it can
        List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x"));
        Bag bag = new Bag(items);
        items.add("y");
        System.out.println("leaky bag = " + bag.items());
 
        // a local record is a named, typed intermediate for a pipeline
        record SkuTotal(String sku, int total) { }
        List<SkuTotal> totals = order.lines().stream()
            .map(l -> new SkuTotal(l.sku(), l.totalInCents()))
            .toList();
        System.out.println("per line  = " + totals);
    }
}
Expected output
toString  = OrderLine[sku=BOLT-7, qty=10, unitPriceInCents=80]
equals    = true, same hash = true
accessor  = BOLT-7 x10
rejected  = qty must be positive: 0
totals    = 900c and 900c (the copy did not change)
nested eq = true
map keys  = 1, picks of BOLT-7 = 2
leaky bag = [x, y]
per line  = [SkuTotal[sku=BOLT-7, total=800], SkuTotal[sku=NUT-3, total=100]]

Read the first three output lines against the highlighted record. " bolt-7 " went in; BOLT-7 came out, because the compact constructor normalised the parameter and the compiler-generated assignment this.sku = sku ran afterwards. Two lines built from different input strings are equal and share a hash code, because both derived members use the normalised fields. And nested eq is true because record equality recurses: Order.equals compares its Address with Address.equals and its List with List.equals, element by element.

The red line is the counter-example. Bag stores the caller's ArrayList as-is, so the caller's later add is visible through bag.items(). The record's reference is final; the object it refers to is whatever you put there. Order avoids this with List.copyOf, which is both a copy and immutable — and is a no-op when handed a list that is already immutable, so the of factory's List.of costs nothing extra.

What the compiler writes for you

record OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) { }

The header is the whole state. Components are listed once and become fields, constructor parameters, accessors and the members of equals/hashCode/toString, in that order.

final class OrderLine extends java.lang.Record {
    private final String sku;
    private final int qty;
    private final int unitPriceInCents;
 
    OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) {   // canonical constructor
        this.sku = sku; this.qty = qty; this.unitPriceInCents = unitPriceInCents;
    }
    public String sku() { return sku; }                       // accessors: no "get" prefix
    public int qty() { return qty; }
    public int unitPriceInCents() { return unitPriceInCents; }
 
    public boolean equals(Object o) { /* same class and every component equal */ }
    public int hashCode()           { /* combined from every component */ }
    public String toString()        { /* OrderLine[sku=…, qty=…, unitPriceInCents=…] */ }
}

Every one of these may be declared explicitly to override the generated version. Do it for an accessor that must return a defensive copy, or a toString that must hide a secret — and never for equals unless you can state why two records with equal components should be unequal.

// Canonical: full parameter list, you MUST assign every field yourself
record OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) {
    OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) {
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty");
        this.sku = sku.strip();
        this.qty = qty;
        this.unitPriceInCents = unitPriceInCents;
    }
}
 
// Compact: no parameter list, parameters are in scope, fields are assigned
// from the (possibly reassigned) parameters AFTER your body runs
record OrderLine(String sku, int qty, int unitPriceInCents) {
    OrderLine {
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty");
        sku = sku.strip();          // legal: it is the parameter
        // this.sku = sku;          // compile error: the field is assigned for you
    }
}

Use the compact form unless you need to do something the automatic assignment cannot. Any other constructor you add (a two-argument convenience, say) must delegate with this(…) to the canonical one, so validation runs exactly once on every path.

Put the compact constructor in order

Five lines of a validating, normalising compact constructor for Address. Order them so that the record can never hold a blank city and always stores the country code in upper case. Remember that the compact body has no parameter list and never assigns this.x.

  1. 1 country = country.strip().toUpperCase();
  2. 2 }
  3. 3 Address {
  4. 4 if (country.length() != 2) throw new IllegalArgumentException("ISO country code required");
  5. 5 if (city == null || city.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("city required");

Correct. Validate the cheap, independent condition first; normalise country before checking its length, so " gb " is accepted as GB rather than rejected for its padding. The implicit this.city = city; this.country = country; runs after the closing brace, picking up the normalised parameter. Swapping lines 3 and 4 would also compile — but then " gb " would throw.

The rules, and the reasons

Record restrictions and their rationale
RuleBecause
No instance fields beyond the componentsThe header must be the complete state, or the generated equals would be wrong. Static fields are allowed.
Implicitly final; cannot be abstractA subclass could add state the header does not know about.
Cannot extends anythingEvery record already extends java.lang.Record. It may implement interfaces, including Comparable.
Components are final; no setters are generatedImmutability is the point. "Change" one by constructing a new record — withQty(int) style methods are a common addition.
Accessors are name(), not getName()A deliberate break from the JavaBeans convention; frameworks that reflect on getters have mostly caught up.
Native methods are forbidden; instance initialiser blocks are forbiddenAll initialisation must be visible in the constructor.
May be nested, local, or generic: record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second)A nested record is implicitly static; a local one cannot capture locals from the enclosing method.

When not to use one

  • The thing has identity. A Customer whose name can change is still the same customer; two records with equal components are indistinguishable by design. If "same object" matters, it is a class.
  • The thing changes. InventoryService mutates. A record of its state could be a snapshot, but the service itself is a class.
  • It needs a superclass. Records cannot extend. Share behaviour through an interface with default methods (§3) or composition.
  • It is a JPA entity or a framework bean that requires a no-argument constructor and setters. Records have neither, by design.
  • Some components are derived. If total is always qty * price, it is a method, not a component — otherwise two lines can disagree with themselves and equals will notice.

What is left — DTOs, map keys, multi-value returns, stream intermediates, configuration values, messages, coordinates, money — is most of the small classes in any codebase. And because a record's components are exactly its accessors, the pattern-matching switch in §9 can take one apart: case OrderLine(var sku, var qty, var price) is only possible because the compiler knows the record's shape.

Record gotchas
  • Immutability is shallow. A component of type List, array or Date is a reference, and the record cannot stop anyone mutating what it points to. Copy in the compact constructor (List.copyOf, array.clone()) and, for arrays, copy again in the accessor.
  • Arrays make equals useless. The generated equals uses Objects.equals on each component, and for arrays that is identity. A record Row(int[] cells) is never equal to another Row with the same numbers. Use a List.
  • A mutable component breaks hash-based collections. Same lesson as Fundamentals §10: if a component's own hashCode can change, the record's can, and a HashSet loses it.
  • Overriding an accessor changes toString but not equals. equals and hashCode read the fields directly, not the accessors. An accessor that returns a copy is fine; one that returns something different from the field makes the record lie.
  • Adding a component is a breaking change for every caller. The canonical constructor's signature changes. Keep a static factory or an explicit convenience constructor as the public entry point if the shape is likely to evolve.

Check yourself

1.Inside a compact constructor you write this.sku = sku.strip();. What happens?

B. In a compact constructor the fields are definitely assigned by the compiler at the end of the body, so assigning this.sku yourself is an error ("cannot assign a value to final variable"). The idiom is to reassign the parameter — sku = sku.strip(); — which the automatic assignment then picks up.

A describes the canonical (full-parameter-list) constructor, where you do assign fields yourself. C would be a terrible design and is not what happens — the compiler rejects the code instead. D is wrong: any statement is allowed, including logging, normalisation and computation; only field assignment is reserved.

2.record Order(long id, List<OrderLine> lines) { } with no explicit constructor. A caller does var l = new ArrayList<OrderLine>(); var o = new Order(1, l); l.add(line);. What is o.lines().size()?

C. The generated canonical constructor is a plain this.lines = lines. The record's field is final, but it refers to the caller's ArrayList, which the caller can still change. This is the Bag case from the worked example. A compact constructor with lines = List.copyOf(lines); is the fix, and it is the first thing to write for any record with a collection component.

A and B credit records with behaviour they do not have — nothing is copied or frozen unless you write it. D is wrong: a component can be any type, which is exactly why shallow immutability is a trap.

3.Which of these should not be a record?

A. A cart mutates and has identity — two carts with the same contents are two different customers' carts. You could model it as a record holding a mutable list, but then its equals and hashCode change under it, and nothing about it is "transparent immutable data". It is a class.

B, C and D are textbook records: values with no identity, compared by content, never changed after construction. D is the interesting one — the stock changes, but a snapshot of it does not, and a record is the right way to say so.

Section 9

Sealed types, switch expressions and pattern matching

Fundamentals §8 taught the object-oriented answer to "the behaviour depends on the type": put the method on the type and let dynamic dispatch choose. That works beautifully when the set of operations is fixed and the set of types keeps growing. The warehouse's pricing rules are the opposite shape: there are three kinds of Discount and there will be three next year, but the operations on them multiply — price a line, describe it on a receipt, decide whether two offers may stack, export it to the accounting system. Putting all of those on each record class scatters one business concept across many files.

Java 21 gives you the other answer. A sealed type declares exactly which subtypes exist, and a pattern-matching switch handles each one in a single place, with the compiler proving that no case has been forgotten. This section is about that pair, and about the switch expression and pattern syntax that make it work.

Sealing a hierarchy

sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne {}
 
record PercentOff(int percent) implements Discount {}       // records are implicitly final
record FixedOff(int cents)     implements Discount {}
record BuyNGetOne(int n)       implements Discount {}
 
sealed class Shipment permits Parcel, Freight {}
final class Parcel extends Shipment {}                      // a permitted subclass must say what it is:
non-sealed class Freight extends Shipment {}                // final, sealed, or non-sealed (open again)
  • Every permitted subtype must be final, sealed or non-sealed. A record or enum is already final.
  • The permitted subtypes must live in the same package as the sealed type (or the same named module). If they are all in the same source file you may omit permits and the compiler infers it.
  • Sealing says nothing about instances: there may be a million PercentOff objects. It constrains the set of classes, which is what exhaustiveness checking needs.

Worked example

Pricing a line under any discount, plus a nested record pattern that takes an OrderLine and the Product inside it apart in one expression.

javaSealedSwitch.java
import java.util.List;
 
public class SealedSwitch {
 
    record Product(String sku, int priceInCents) {}
    record Line(Product product, int qty) {}
 
    sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne {}
    record PercentOff(int percent) implements Discount {
        PercentOff {
            if (percent < 0 || percent > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percent out of range: " + percent);
        }
    }
    record FixedOff(int cents) implements Discount {}
    record BuyNGetOne(int n) implements Discount {}
 
    static int lineTotal(Line line, Discount discount) {
        int gross = line.product().priceInCents() * line.qty();
        return switch (discount) {                              // no default: the compiler knows every case
            case PercentOff(int pct)                     -> gross - gross * pct / 100;
            case FixedOff(int cents) when cents >= gross -> 0;  // guard: a voucher never goes negative
            case FixedOff(int cents)                     -> gross - cents;
            case BuyNGetOne(int n)                       -> gross - (line.qty() / (n + 1)) * line.product().priceInCents();
        };
    }
 
    static String describe(Line line) {
        // a nested record pattern takes the line AND the product inside it apart in one go
        if (line instanceof Line(Product(String sku, int price), int qty) && qty > 1) {
            return qty + " x " + sku + " @ " + price + "c";
        }
        return "single " + line.product().sku();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Line bolts = new Line(new Product("BOLT-7", 80), 10);
        List<Discount> offers = List.of(new PercentOff(10), new FixedOff(100), new FixedOff(5_000), new BuyNGetOne(4));
        for (Discount d : offers) {
            System.out.printf("%-20s -> %4d%n", d, lineTotal(bolts, d));
        }
        System.out.println(describe(bolts));
        System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Product("GIRD-1", 120_000), 1)));
    }
}
Expected output
PercentOff[percent=10] ->  720
FixedOff[cents=100]  ->  700
FixedOff[cents=5000] ->    0
BuyNGetOne[n=4]      ->  640
10 x BOLT-7 @ 80c
single GIRD-1

Four things to notice in lineTotal. It is a switch expression: it produces the value that return hands back, so there is no mutable result variable and no way to forget an assignment. Each case is a record pattern: PercentOff(int pct) both tests the type and binds the component, so the body never calls an accessor. The when clause is a guard: the first FixedOff case applies only when the voucher is worth more than the line, and because it comes first, the second FixedOff case is reached only when the guard failed. And there is no default, which is not laziness but the whole point.

Exhaustiveness: let the compiler count

A switch expression must yield a value for every possible input, so the compiler checks that the cases cover the type. For an int or a String that is impossible without default. For an enum or a sealed type the compiler knows the complete set of values or subtypes and can verify coverage itself. Try breaking it:

What javac says about this switch
Cases present
Hierarchy and fallback

The lesson the sandbox is making: a default on a sealed switch does not add safety, it removes it. Without one, adding a subtype breaks every switch that needs updating, at compile time, with the file and line. With one, the new subtype silently takes the fallback path in production.

Switch: statement, expression, and the pattern forms

// statement: does things, yields nothing, need not be exhaustive (unless it uses patterns)
switch (sku) {
    case "BOLT-7", "NUT-3" -> band = "small";
    default                -> band = "standard";
}
 
// expression: IS a value, must be exhaustive, every branch yields the same kind of thing
String band = switch (sku) {
    case "BOLT-7", "NUT-3" -> "small";
    default                -> "standard";
};

Prefer the expression whenever the switch exists to compute something. It cannot forget a branch, cannot leave a variable unassigned, and reads as the single thing it is. One subtlety: a switch statement that uses patterns (type or record patterns, or case null) must also be exhaustive, so the old "it compiles with cases missing" behaviour applies only to the legacy constant forms.

int days = switch (category) {
    case FASTENER   -> 1;                 // arrow: one expression, no fall-through, no break
    case STRUCTURAL -> 14;
    case TOOLING    -> {                  // arrow with a block: must yield
        int base = 3;
        yield base * 2;
    }
};
 
int legacy = switch (category) {          // colon form in an expression: fall-through still exists
    case FASTENER:
    case STRUCTURAL: yield 7;             // both labels reach this yield
    default:         yield 0;
};

Use the arrow form. Fall-through, the reason every C-family language has a "forgot the break" bug, is impossible with arrows: each case is a self-contained expression or block. yield exists only to get a value out of a block; it is not return and will not leave the enclosing method.

Pattern kinds and what they bind
PatternExampleBinds
Type patterncase String s ->s, the value cast to String
Record patterncase FixedOff(int cents) ->each component, by position
Nested record patterncase Line(Product(var sku, var p), int qty) ->components at every level; var infers the type
Guarded patterncase FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross ->as above, only if the guard is true
Null casecase null -> or case null, default ->nothing; without it a null selector throws NullPointerException

A type pattern on instanceof works the same way: if (o instanceof String s) tests and binds in one step, and s is in scope wherever the compiler can prove the test passed, including after an early return in the negated form.

Patterns outside the sealed case

Patterns are not only for sealed types. The same machinery handles Object, enums, strings and primitives, with dominance rules that decide which case may come first.

javaPatterns.java
public class Patterns {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, TOOLING }
 
    static String classify(Object o) {
        return switch (o) {
            case null                 -> "null, handled as a case: no NullPointerException";
            case Integer i when i < 0 -> "negative int " + i;
            case Integer i            -> "int " + i;
            case String s             -> "string of length " + s.length();
            case int[] arr            -> "int array of " + arr.length;
            default                   -> "something else: " + o.getClass().getSimpleName();
        };
    }
 
    static int leadTimeDays(Category c) {
        return switch (c) {                 // exhaustive over the enum: no default needed
            case FASTENER   -> 1;
            case STRUCTURAL -> 14;
            case TOOLING    -> {            // a block body must yield its value
                int base = 3;
                yield base * 2;
            }
        };
    }
 
    static String shippingBand(String sku) {
        switch (sku) {                      // the statement form: no value, no exhaustiveness check
            case "BOLT-7", "NUT-3" -> { return "small"; }
            case "GIRD-1"          -> { return "freight"; }
            default                -> { return "standard"; }
        }
    }
 
    static String label(Object o) {
        if (!(o instanceof String s)) return "not a string";
        return "string " + s.toUpperCase();   // s is in scope: the compiler saw the early return
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(classify(null));
        System.out.println(classify(-4));
        System.out.println(classify(42));
        System.out.println(classify("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println(classify(new int[3]));
        System.out.println(classify(3.5));
        for (Category c : Category.values()) System.out.println(c + " -> " + leadTimeDays(c) + " days");
        System.out.println(shippingBand("NUT-3") + ", " + shippingBand("GIRD-1") + ", " + shippingBand("CAM-9"));
        System.out.println(label("rod-4") + " / " + label(7));
    }
}
Expected output
null, handled as a case: no NullPointerException
negative int -4
int 42
string of length 6
int array of 3
something else: Double
FASTENER -> 1 days
STRUCTURAL -> 14 days
TOOLING -> 6 days
small, freight, standard
string ROD-4 / not a string

The order of the two Integer cases is not a style choice. A case that would match everything a later case matches dominates it, and the compiler rejects the program: swap them and you get error: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label, because the guarded case could never be reached. The same rule puts case CharSequence cs after case String s, never before. default is exempt and may appear anywhere, though convention keeps it last.

In label, the pattern variable s is usable on the line after the if. The compiler reasons about flow: the only way past that statement is for the instanceof to have succeeded, so the binding is in scope. The same reasoning allows o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3, because && evaluates its right side only when the left was true, and forbids o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty(), where the right side runs exactly when s does not exist.

Five ways this goes wrong
  • A pattern switch throws on null unless you say otherwise. The legacy forms did too, but a case Object o looks like it would catch anything and does not. Write case null explicitly, or case null, default to merge the two.
  • A guard is not a case. case FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross covers some FixedOff values. You still need an unguarded FixedOff case, or the switch is not exhaustive and the error message names the type you thought you had handled.
  • Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time against the classes the compiler saw. If a sealed interface is recompiled with a new subtype but a dependent jar is not, the old switch is still exhaustive as far as its bytecode knows. At runtime the JVM throws MatchException from the switch, which is the correct, loud failure; just do not mistake "it compiled last year" for proof.
  • Record patterns match on type, not on accessor calls. case Product(String sku, int price) invokes the accessors to bind, so an accessor you overrode to compute something runs during matching. Keep accessors cheap and side-effect free.
  • yield inside a lambda inside a switch block does not yield from the switch. It is a statement with its own scope rules; the compiler will tell you, but the error is confusing until you know why.

Sealed switch or polymorphic method?

When to prefer a sealed switch over a polymorphic method
The situationReach forBecause
Types keep being added; the operations are few and stable (shapes in a drawing app)Polymorphism: an abstract method on the supertypeA new type is one new class, and nothing else changes
Types are fixed and known; operations keep being added (discount kinds; AST nodes; messages)A sealed type and pattern switchesA new operation is one new method, and the compiler lists every switch when a type is eventually added
The operation needs data from several types at once (do these two offers stack?)A switch over a record of both, or nested patternsDispatch on one receiver cannot see the other's concrete type
The behaviour belongs to the type's own invariants (validation, formatting of itself)A method on the recordIt changes when the record changes, and nowhere else

Both tools solve one axis of the expression problem, which is the observation that no single design makes both adding types and adding operations cheap. The practical rule: ask which one will change more often in this hierarchy, and put the compiler's checking on that axis.

Check yourself

1.A switch expression over sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne has cases for all three and no default. A colleague adds record Clearance() implements Discount and Clearance to the permits list. What happens to the switch?

B. That compile error is the feature. The sealed type tells the compiler the complete set of subtypes; the switch expression must cover it; the new subtype is uncovered; the build fails at every switch that needs a Clearance rule, with file and line.

A is what happens only in the separate-compilation case, when the switch's class file predates the new subtype and is not rebuilt; a normal build recompiles it. C invents a warning; exhaustiveness is an error, never a warning. D confuses the interface, which has no behaviour, with a case label.

2.Which of these fails to compile?

C. Every String is a CharSequence, so the first case matches everything the second could, and the second is unreachable. The compiler reports that the label is dominated by a preceding one.

A is the correct order for a guard: the narrower, guarded case first, the unguarded one as the catch-all for that type. B is the same pair as C in the legal order, specific before general. D is legal and is the idiom for "handle null together with anything I did not list".

3.For which of these can the compiler verify that a switch expression is exhaustive without a default? Select all that apply.

A and D. Exhaustiveness needs a closed set that the compiler can enumerate: an enum's constants, or a sealed type's permitted subtypes (recursively, if those are sealed too). Record patterns count as covering their record type when every component pattern is total, as int cents is.

B: the set of strings is infinite and the compiler has no idea which ones are "current SKUs"; a default is mandatory. C: an open interface may gain an implementation in any jar at any time, so three cases today prove nothing; the compiler will demand a default, which is also the hint that you may want to seal the interface.

Section 10

Comparable, Comparator and immutability

Two ideas that look unrelated and are not. Ordering is a contract: compareTo promises things about every pair of values, and TreeSet, TreeMap and every sort rely on those promises without checking them. Immutability is the strongest way to keep such contracts true, because a value that cannot change cannot drift out of the order it was inserted under, cannot be mutated by one caller behind another's back, and can be shared and cached without a second thought. The warehouse reports in §5 and §6 sort products and group them; this section is what makes that safe.

Comparable: the natural order

A class implements Comparable<T> to say "my instances have one obvious ordering". String compares lexicographically, Integer numerically, LocalDate chronologically. The method returns a negative number, zero or a positive number, and must obey three rules for every a, b and c:

  • Antisymmetry: sgn(a.compareTo(b)) == -sgn(b.compareTo(a)). If a < b then b > a.
  • Transitivity: a < b and b < c imply a < c. A sort that gets inconsistent answers may loop or throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract.
  • Consistency with equals, strongly recommended: a.compareTo(b) == 0 exactly when a.equals(b). Sorted collections use compareTo to decide duplicates, so when the two disagree, a TreeSet and a HashSet hold different elements for the same input.

Worked example

javaSorting.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;
 
public class Sorting {
 
    static final class Product implements Comparable<Product> {
        private final String sku;
        private final int priceInCents;
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        @Override public int compareTo(Product o) { return sku.compareTo(o.sku); }   // natural order: by SKU
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Product> cart = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Product("NUT-3", 25), new Product("BOLT-7", 80),
                new Product("CAM-9", 80), new Product("ROD-4", 300)));
 
        Collections.sort(cart);                                      // natural order via compareTo
        System.out.println("natural           " + cart);
 
        cart.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Product::priceInCents));   // stable: BOLT-7 stays before CAM-9
        System.out.println("by price (stable) " + cart);
 
        cart.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::priceInCents).thenComparing(Product::sku).reversed());
        System.out.println("(price,sku) rev   " + cart);
 
        cart.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::priceInCents, Comparator.reverseOrder()).thenComparing(Product::sku));
        System.out.println("price desc, sku   " + cart);
 
        List<String> skus = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("NUT-3", null, "BOLT-7"));
        skus.sort(Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println("nulls first       " + skus);
 
        // a comparator inconsistent with equals: the set treats equal-priced products as duplicates
        Set<Product> byPrice = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Product::priceInCents));
        byPrice.addAll(cart);
        System.out.println("TreeSet by price  " + byPrice + "  size=" + byPrice.size() + " of " + cart.size());
 
        int a = Integer.MAX_VALUE, b = -1;
        System.out.println("a - b             " + (a - b) + "  (overflow: wrong sign)");
        System.out.println("Integer.compare   " + Integer.compare(a, b));
    }
}
Expected output
natural           [BOLT-7@80, CAM-9@80, NUT-3@25, ROD-4@300]
by price (stable) [NUT-3@25, BOLT-7@80, CAM-9@80, ROD-4@300]
(price,sku) rev   [ROD-4@300, CAM-9@80, BOLT-7@80, NUT-3@25]
price desc, sku   [ROD-4@300, BOLT-7@80, CAM-9@80, NUT-3@25]
nulls first       [null, BOLT-7, NUT-3]
TreeSet by price  [NUT-3@25, BOLT-7@80, ROD-4@300]  size=3 of 4
a - b             -2147483648  (overflow: wrong sign)
Integer.compare   1

Line 29 shows a stable sort: BOLT-7 and CAM-9 both cost 80, and they keep the relative order they had before. Every object sort in the JDK is stable, which is what makes "sort by category, then by price" achievable as two successive sorts as well as one chained comparator. Lines 32 and 35 produce different results from what look like the same ingredients; the reason is the gotcha below. Line 43 silently drops CAM-9: the comparator says it is "equal" to BOLT-7, and a set keeps one of each. The last two lines are why you never write return a - b in a comparator: the subtraction overflows, and Integer.compare does not.

Building comparators

Comparator factory and combinator methods
MethodProducesNote
Comparator.comparing(keyFn)order by a Comparable keycomparing(Product::sku)
comparing(keyFn, keyCmp)order by a key using a second comparatorthe clean way to say "price descending, then sku ascending"
comparingInt / Long / Doubleprimitive key, no boxingprefer for numeric fields
.thenComparing(…)tie-breaker applied only when the previous compare returned 0chains indefinitely; also has thenComparingInt
.reversed()the opposite of everything built so farsee the gotcha
Comparator.naturalOrder() / reverseOrder()the element's own compareTo, or its reversetyped; needs a Comparable element
nullsFirst(cmp) / nullsLast(cmp)a comparator that tolerates nullseverything else throws NullPointerException on a null element
reversed() reverses the whole chain, not the last key

comparing(price).thenComparing(sku).reversed() means "the reverse of (price, then sku)": price descending and sku descending, which is why line 32 printed CAM-9 before BOLT-7. It is a method on the comparator you have built so far, so it cannot know you meant only the last key. To reverse one key, reverse that key's comparator: comparing(price, reverseOrder()).thenComparing(sku), as on line 35.

A second trap in the same family: Comparator.comparing(Product::priceInCents).reversed() compiles, but Comparator.comparing(p -> p.priceInCents()).reversed() does not. With a lambda the compiler cannot infer p's type before it sees reversed(), which gives it nothing to go on. A method reference carries the type; a lambda needs Comparator.comparing((Product p) -> …).

Where sorting happens

cart.sort(null);                       // natural order (List.sort, Java 8+): sorts in place
cart.sort(byPrice);                    // same, with a comparator
Collections.sort(cart);                // the older spelling; delegates to list.sort

Both sort in place using TimSort: a stable merge sort that runs in O(n) on already-sorted or nearly-sorted input and O(n log n) otherwise. An immutable list (List.of) throws UnsupportedOperationException; copy it first.

int[] prices = { 300, 25, 80, 80 };
Arrays.sort(prices);                   // dual-pivot quicksort: fast, NOT stable, primitives only
 
Product[] items = …;
Arrays.sort(items, byPrice);           // TimSort: stable, any Comparator
Arrays.parallelSort(items, byPrice);   // splits across cores; worth it from ~10⁴ elements

Stability is meaningless for primitives, since two equal ints are indistinguishable, so the JDK uses a faster unstable algorithm for them. For objects it must preserve order among "equal" elements and uses TimSort.

List<Product> cheapest = cart.stream().sorted(byPrice).limit(3).toList();   // a new list; source untouched
 
Set<Product> ordered = new TreeSet<>(byPrice);     // kept sorted on every insert, O(log n) each
Map<String, Integer> stock = new TreeMap<>();      // sorted by key; needs Comparable keys or a comparator

sorted() on a stream is a stateful operation: it must see every element before it can emit the first one, so it buffers the whole stream (§5). A TreeSet keeps its order incrementally and is the right choice when elements arrive over time and you repeatedly need the smallest, the largest, or a range.

Immutability: unmodifiable is not immutable

Java has two ideas that are easy to confuse. An unmodifiable view is a wrapper that refuses writes through itself but shows whatever its underlying collection currently holds. An immutable collection owns its elements, has no underlying collection, and cannot change through any reference. The difference is invisible until someone keeps a reference to the original.

javaImmutable.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Immutable {
 
    static final class Order {
        private final List<String> skus;                          // final reference to a mutable object
        Order(List<String> skus) { this.skus = new ArrayList<>(skus); }        // defensive copy in
        List<String> skus() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(skus); }     // read-only view out
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> source = new ArrayList<>(List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3"));
        List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
        List<String> copy = List.copyOf(source);
 
        source.add("CAM-9");
        System.out.println("source " + source);
        System.out.println("view   " + view + "   a view: it follows the source");
        System.out.println("copy   " + copy + "   a snapshot: fixed at copy time");
 
        try { view.add("ROD-4"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("view.add            -> UnsupportedOperationException"); }
 
        try { List.of("BOLT-7", null); }
        catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("List.of(.., null)   -> NullPointerException"); }
 
        List<String> input = new ArrayList<>(List.of("PIN-2"));
        Order order = new Order(input);
        input.add("HUB-8");                                       // the caller keeps mutating its own list
        System.out.println("order  " + order.skus() + "   unaffected: the constructor copied");
 
        try { order.skus().add("HUB-8"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("order.skus().add    -> UnsupportedOperationException"); }
 
        System.out.println("List.copyOf(copy) == copy ? " + (List.copyOf(copy) == copy) + "   already immutable, so no new object");
    }
}
Expected output
source [BOLT-7, NUT-3, CAM-9]
view   [BOLT-7, NUT-3, CAM-9]   a view: it follows the source
copy   [BOLT-7, NUT-3]   a snapshot: fixed at copy time
view.add            -> UnsupportedOperationException
List.of(.., null)   -> NullPointerException
order  [PIN-2]   unaffected: the constructor copied
order.skus().add    -> UnsupportedOperationException
List.copyOf(copy) == copy ? true   already immutable, so no new object

Watch the three references diverge

View, copy, and the source they came from Simulated ← → to step
Source
List<String> source = new ArrayList<>(List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3"));
List<String> view   = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
List<String> copy   = List.copyOf(source);
 
source.add("CAM-9");
System.out.println(view);
System.out.println(copy);
 
view.add("ROD-4");
copy.add("ROD-4");
What each reference sees
Standard output

The three rules of an immutable class

  1. Every field is private final and set once, in the constructor. final on a field means the reference cannot be reassigned. It says nothing about the object at the other end, which is why rule 2 exists.
  2. Mutable inputs are copied on the way in, and either copied or wrapped on the way out. The Order above copies the list in its constructor, so a caller who keeps mutating their own list cannot reach inside. Its accessor returns an unmodifiable view, which is safe here precisely because nobody else holds the private list. A Date or an array needs the same treatment; a String, a record of primitives, or a List.copyOf result does not, because they are already immutable.
  3. The class is final, or its constructors are private. Otherwise a subclass can add mutable state and override methods, and code that trusts "an Order never changes" is trusting something a subclass can break. Records satisfy all three rules by construction, which is why §8 recommends them for this job.

Immutable collections from List.of, Set.of, Map.of and the copyOf methods add three behaviours of their own: they reject null elements and keys, they are value-based (never compare them with ==; the JDK may return the same instance or a new one as it sees fit, as the last line of the program shows), and Set.of and Map.of deliberately randomise iteration order per JVM run so that no code can accidentally depend on it.

Match the need to the API

Drag an API onto the situation it solves, or click one then the other

All four correct. The two list APIs differ only in whether the result follows the source; the two comparator APIs are the fixes for the two most common comparator bugs, a NullPointerException from a null element and a reversed() that reversed too much.

Gotchas worth a second read
  • A sorted collection with a comparator inconsistent with equals loses elements. TreeSet asks the comparator, never equals, whether two elements are the same. If you want "sort by price but keep every product", sort a list; if you need a set, give the comparator a tie-breaker that only returns 0 for genuinely equal elements: comparingInt(price).thenComparing(sku).
  • Mutating an element after inserting it into a TreeSet corrupts the tree. The element sits where its old key put it; lookups by the new key miss, and the set may now contain "duplicates". The same disease as a mutable HashMap key (§11), and the same cure: immutable keys.
  • final is not immutability. private final List<String> skus = new ArrayList<>() prevents skus = other and nothing else. skus.add(…) still compiles and still runs.
  • Arrays.asList is fixed-size but not immutable. set works and writes through to the array; add throws. It is neither a copy nor a true view in the sense above.
  • Equal by compareTo, unequal by equals breaks Collections.sort expectations too. BigDecimal is the famous case: new BigDecimal("1.0") and new BigDecimal("1.00") compare as 0 but are not equals, so a HashSet holds both and a TreeSet holds one.

Check yourself

1.You want products ordered by price descending, and among equal prices by SKU ascending. Which comparator does that?

C. Reverse the price key alone by giving comparing a reversed key comparator, then add the ascending tie-breaker. Nothing after it is affected.

A reverses both keys: price descending, sku descending. B reverses twice, which puts price back to ascending and sku to descending, the exact opposite of what was asked. D sorts primarily by sku, with price as the tie-breaker, and then reverses both.

2.Order stores private final List<String> skus, assigned straight from the constructor parameter, and exposes it with return skus;. A caller does List<String> mine = new ArrayList<>(); Order o = new Order(mine); mine.add("X");. What does o.skus() now contain, and what is the fix?

B. The field and the caller's variable point at the same ArrayList. The defensive copy on the way in gives Order its own list; the view or copy on the way out stops callers writing to it.

A is the classic misunderstanding: final fixes the reference, not the object. C wraps the caller's list in a view, so the caller's later add still shows through; a view protects against writes through itself only. D confuses this with iterator fail-fast behaviour, which needs an iteration in progress.

3.Four products are added to new TreeSet<>(comparingInt(Product::priceInCents)). Two of them cost 80. What is the set's size and why?

D. A sorted set has no hash table and never calls equals or hashCode. Its only notion of "same element" is a comparator result of zero, so the second 80-cent product is silently not added. This is what "consistent with equals" guards against.

A and B both assume equals is consulted; it is not. C: the comparator is perfectly valid. Returning 0 for distinct objects is allowed by the contract; it is merely inconsistent with equals, which the documentation warns about but cannot detect.

Section 11

Inside the collections

Fundamentals §12 told you which collection to pick and what each operation costs. This section opens them up, because the costs are not laws of nature: they hold only while certain conditions do. HashMap.get is O(1) only if the hash function spreads keys and the key never changes. ArrayList.add is O(1) only on average, with occasional O(n) pauses. Knowing the mechanism is what lets you predict when the guarantee is about to break, and the warehouse's stock map, keyed by SKU and consulted on every pick, is exactly where that prediction matters.

HashMap, one put at a time

A HashMap is an array of bins (the table), each holding zero or more entries. Putting a key means finding its bin, then checking the entries already there:

int h = key.hashCode();                 // 1. the key's own 32-bit hash
h = h ^ (h >>> 16);                     // 2. "spread": fold the high bits into the low ones
int index = (table.length - 1) & h;     // 3. the bin: a mask, not a modulo, because length is a power of 2
// 4. walk the bin: an entry with the same hash AND key.equals(existing) means replace, else append
  • Step 3 only uses the low bits of h, which is why step 2 exists: a hashCode whose variation is all in the high bits (think of keys that are multiples of 65536) would otherwise collide into one bin.
  • Each bin is a linked list of entries. Once a bin holds 8 entries and the table has at least 64 bins, the list is converted to a red-black tree so that lookups in that bin become O(log n) instead of O(n). This is the JDK defending itself against a bad hashCode; it needs the keys to be Comparable to do a good job.
  • The full hash is stored in each entry, so the walk compares ints first and calls equals only on a hash match. A cheap hashCode and an exact equals is the pair the structure is built for.

Load factor and resizing

Bins fill up as entries arrive, and long bins make every operation slower. So the map tracks a threshold, capacity × loadFactor, and when the entry count exceeds it the table doubles and every entry is re-inserted. The default load factor of 0.75 is the trade-off the JDK authors settled on: on average under one entry per bin, with the table only a third empty. Watch what that costs as a map grows.

Grow a HashMap and watch it resize

Three consequences follow from the resize rule. The amortised cost of put is still O(1), because doublings are geometric: a map that reached 200 entries did about 200 + 100 + 50 + … ≈ 400 re-insertions in total, not 200 × 200. A map whose size you know in advance should be created with that capacity (divided by the load factor), which skips every resize. And iteration order changes on resize: entries move to new bins when the mask gains a bit, so code that "worked" because a HashMap happened to iterate in insertion order breaks the day it grows past 12 entries.

Worked example

The mutable-key failure, three idioms that replace get-check-put, the ordered maps, and the fail-fast iterator, all in one program.

javaMapInternals.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.ConcurrentModificationException;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
 
public class MapInternals {
 
    static final class Bin {                        // a mutable key: the mistake this section is about
        String code;
        Bin(String code) { this.code = code; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Bin b && b.code.equals(code); }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return code.hashCode(); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Bin, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
        Bin key = new Bin("A-01");
        stock.put(key, 40);
        key.code = "A-02";                           // the hash changes; the entry stays in the old bucket
        System.out.println("size=" + stock.size()
                + "  containsKey(A-01)=" + stock.containsKey(new Bin("A-01"))
                + "  containsKey(A-02)=" + stock.containsKey(new Bin("A-02"))
                + "  containsKey(key)=" + stock.containsKey(key));
 
        Map<String, List<String>> byCategory = new TreeMap<>();
        byCategory.computeIfAbsent("FASTENER", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("BOLT-7");
        byCategory.computeIfAbsent("FASTENER", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("NUT-3");
        byCategory.computeIfAbsent("STRUCTURAL", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("GIRD-1");
        System.out.println("multimap  " + byCategory);
 
        Map<String, Integer> picks = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String sku : List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "BOLT-7", "BOLT-7")) picks.merge(sku, 1, Integer::sum);
        System.out.println("counts    " + picks + "  CAM-9 -> " + picks.getOrDefault("CAM-9", 0));
 
        Map<String, Integer> linked = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> sorted = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String sku : List.of("ROD-4", "BOLT-7", "NUT-3")) { linked.put(sku, 1); sorted.put(sku, 1); }
        System.out.println("linked    " + linked.keySet() + "  insertion order");
        System.out.println("tree      " + sorted.keySet() + "  sorted order");
 
        TreeMap<Integer, String> bands = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(0, "small", 100, "medium", 1_000, "large"));
        System.out.println("250c is " + bands.floorEntry(250).getValue() + ", bands under 1000: " + bands.headMap(1_000).keySet());
 
        Map<String, Integer> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {   // true = access order
            @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, Integer> e) { return size() > 2; }
        };
        lru.put("BOLT-7", 1); lru.put("NUT-3", 1);
        lru.get("BOLT-7");                           // touching it makes NUT-3 the eldest
        lru.put("CAM-9", 1);
        System.out.println("lru       " + lru.keySet() + "  NUT-3 evicted: least recently used");
 
        List<String> toShip = new ArrayList<>(List.of("BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9", "ROD-4"));
        try {
            for (String s : toShip) if (s.startsWith("B")) toShip.remove(s);
        } catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
            System.out.println("for-each remove -> ConcurrentModificationException, list now " + toShip);
        }
        toShip.removeIf(s -> s.startsWith("N"));
        for (Iterator<String> it = toShip.iterator(); it.hasNext();) if (it.next().startsWith("C")) it.remove();
        System.out.println("removeIf + Iterator.remove -> " + toShip);
    }
}
Expected output
size=1  containsKey(A-01)=false  containsKey(A-02)=false  containsKey(key)=false
multimap  {FASTENER=[BOLT-7, NUT-3], STRUCTURAL=[GIRD-1]}
counts    {BOLT-7=3, NUT-3=1}  CAM-9 -> 0
linked    [ROD-4, BOLT-7, NUT-3]  insertion order
tree      [BOLT-7, NUT-3, ROD-4]  sorted order
250c is medium, bands under 1000: [0, 100]
lru       [BOLT-7, CAM-9]  NUT-3 evicted: least recently used
for-each remove -> ConcurrentModificationException, list now [NUT-3, CAM-9, ROD-4]
removeIf + Iterator.remove -> [ROD-4]

The first line is the one to stare at. The map holds one entry and cannot find it by any key, including the very object that was used to put it. The entry sits in the bin chosen for the hash of "A-01"; a lookup for "A-02" goes to a different bin, and a lookup for "A-01" reaches the right bin but then fails the equals check against a key that now says "A-02". Nothing throws. The entry is simply unreachable until a resize happens to move it, at which point it may become reachable under the new key, which is worse, because now the behaviour depends on how many other entries exist. The cure is the one §10 gave: keys are immutable, full stop. Records and strings are good keys; anything with a setter is not.

computeIfAbsent (lines 30 to 32) is the idiom for a map of collections: one call creates the list on first sight of the key and returns the existing one afterwards. merge (line 36) is the idiom for counting and summing. Both replace a three-line get, null check, put dance that is easy to get wrong and, on concurrent maps, impossible to make atomic by hand.

The other structures

A plain Object[] plus a size. get(i) is an array read. add writes at size and increments it; when the array is full, a new one of 1.5× the length is allocated and the old contents copied with System.arraycopy. That copy is O(n), but it happens only every 1.5× growth, so the cost per add averages out to O(1): amortised constant time.

  • new ArrayList<>(expected) skips the growth copies. ensureCapacity(n) does the same later; trimToSize() gives back the slack after a bulk load.
  • add(0, x) and remove(0) shift everything: O(n). A queue built on ArrayList is a quadratic accident waiting to happen; use ArrayDeque.
  • Removing never shrinks the array. A list that once held a million elements and now holds ten still owns a million slots until you trimToSize() or replace it.

A ring buffer: an array with a head and tail index that wrap around the end. Adding at either end moves one index; nothing shifts. When the ring is full it doubles and the elements are copied into the new array in order.

  • O(1) at both ends makes it the right stack and the right queue. Stack is a synchronized legacy class; LinkedList pays a node allocation per element and scatters them across the heap.
  • No index access by design: get(i) does not exist, which is the API telling you what the structure is for.
  • Rejects null elements, because poll() returns null to mean "empty".

A red-black tree: a binary search tree that rebalances itself on every insert and delete so that its height stays within 2 log₂ n. Every operation walks from the root, comparing with compareTo or the comparator at each node: O(log n) and never worse, regardless of insertion order.

  • No hashing, no equals, no resizing. Keys must be mutually comparable or the first put throws ClassCastException.
  • Pays for its order with navigation: firstKey, floorEntry(k) (the greatest key ≤ k, used for the price bands above), ceilingKey, headMap, tailMap, subMap. The sub-map views are live: writes to them go into the tree.
  • About 3–5× slower than HashMap for plain lookups and heavier per entry. Pick it for the navigation, not for the sort; a one-off sorted report is cheaper as HashMap plus a sort.

A HashMap whose entries are also threaded onto a doubly linked list. Lookups use the hash table; iteration follows the list, so the order is predictable: insertion order by default, or access order when constructed with the three-argument constructor's true, in which every get moves the entry to the tail.

  • Access order plus an overridden removeEldestEntry is a complete LRU cache in six lines, as the worked example shows.
  • Costs one extra pair of references per entry and slightly slower writes. Iteration is usually faster than HashMap's, which has to skip empty bins.
  • Resizing does not change iteration order, which removes the HashMap surprise described above. Tests that assert on a map's printed form should use this or TreeMap, never HashMap.

Fail-fast iterators

Every collection in java.util keeps a modCount that each structural change increments. An iterator remembers the count it saw at creation and compares on every next(); a mismatch throws ConcurrentModificationException. The name is misleading: no threads are involved, as the worked example shows with a single-threaded loop. The check exists because an iterator over a resized table or a shifted array would otherwise return garbage or skip elements, and a loud failure is preferable.

Ways to modify a collection during iteration
TechniqueSafe?Why
for-each + list.remove(x)NoThe hidden iterator's count no longer matches. Often throws on the next iteration, not the removal itself; removing the second-to-last element throws nothing, because hasNext() returns false first
Iterator.remove()YesThe iterator performs the removal and updates its own expected count
removeIf(predicate)YesOne pass, implemented by the collection itself; also the fastest option on ArrayList
Indexed loop downwards with remove(i)YesRemoval shifts only the elements already visited
Iterate a copy, modify the originalYesTwo collections, two counts; costs a copy
ConcurrentHashMap / CopyOnWriteArrayListYesWeakly consistent iterators: they never throw and reflect some or all changes made since creation. The subject of Java Advanced
Where the O(1) quietly stops being true
  • A constant hashCode is legal and catastrophic. Every key lands in one bin; the map becomes a linked list (or, past 8 entries with a 64-bin table, a tree of keys that must also be Comparable to be ordered well). Lookups go from O(1) to O(n) and nothing warns you.
  • computeIfAbsent must not modify the map inside its function. Doing so throws ConcurrentModificationException since Java 9, because the map is mid-insertion. Compute, then put, if the computation needs other entries.
  • Map.of and Set.of randomise iteration order per JVM run. Deliberately. If a test passes on your machine and fails in CI with the same code, this is a likely reason; it is also the reason none of the verified programs in this module print a HashSet.
  • Collections.unmodifiableMap on a LinkedHashMap keeps the order; Map.copyOf does not. The copy is a plain immutable map with the randomised order above. Use the view, or a TreeMap, when order must survive.
  • ArrayList.remove(int) and remove(Object) are different overloads, and a List<Integer> hits the index version with list.remove(3). Fundamentals §2 warned about it; it is worth repeating because it corrupts data silently.

Check yourself

1.A HashMap was created with default settings and has just received its 13th entry. What happened?
