B. Default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, threshold 12. The 13th entry pushes the size past the threshold, the table doubles, every entry is rehashed into the larger table, and because the index mask gained a bit, entries can move to different bins and iterate in a different order.

A confuses the threshold with the capacity. C is the ArrayList rule; hash tables double so that the mask stays a power of two. D happens only when a single bin reaches 8 entries, which 13 well-spread keys will not do.

2.A Bin object is used as a HashMap key, then one of the fields its hashCode depends on is changed. What is true afterwards?

C. The entry was filed under the old hash's bin. A lookup for the new value goes to a different bin; a lookup for the old value reaches the right bin but fails equals against a key that now holds the new value. The map has no way to know a key changed, so it cannot react.

A: modCount tracks structural changes to the map, not to keys. B: nothing is re-filed except during a resize, and then the entry lands under its current hash, which can make it reappear unpredictably. D: the map does store the reference, and the worked example shows containsKey(key) returning false anyway, because the lookup recomputes the hash from the mutated object first.

3.Which of these remove matching elements from an ArrayList without risking ConcurrentModificationException? Select all that apply.

A, C and D. removeIf is implemented by the list itself in a single pass. Iterator.remove keeps the iterator's expected count in step. A downward indexed loop never uses an iterator and only shifts elements it has already passed.

B is the classic: the for-each hides an iterator, the remove bumps modCount behind its back, and the next next() throws. Worse, if the match is the second-to-last element it does not throw, because hasNext() sees cursor == size and stops, silently skipping the last element. An ascending indexed loop has the sibling bug of skipping the element that slides into the removed slot.

Section 12

Dates and times with java.time

Every order has a placed timestamp, every SLA is a deadline, and every report is a window. Getting those wrong does not throw — it silently ships an order a day late twice a year, or double-counts the hour that happens twice in October. java.time (Java 8) was designed around the two ideas that the older java.util.Date never separated: a point on the timeline is not the same thing as a reading on a wall clock, and the mapping between them depends on a zone whose rules change.

Every type in the package is immutable and thread-safe, every "setter" returns a new value, months are numbered from 1, and arithmetic is explicit about whether it counts calendar units or elapsed seconds. Those four properties are what you are buying; the rest of this section is about using them correctly.

Which type holds what

The core java.time types, what each stores, and what to use it for
TypeStoresZone?Use it for
InstantNanoseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00ZUTC onlyWhen something happened. Store this in the database and in logs.
LocalDateYear, month, daynoneBirthdays, invoice dates, "placed on" — a calendar day with no time of day.
LocalTimeHour, minute, second, nanononeOpening hours, a daily cut-off — a wall-clock time with no date.
LocalDateTimeDate + timenoneA reading off a wall clock whose zone is known from context. Ambiguous on its own — it cannot be converted to an Instant without a zone.
ZonedDateTimeDate + time + ZoneId + offsetregion rulesA future appointment in a place. Adjusts itself when DST rules apply.
OffsetDateTimeDate + time + fixed offsetfixed offsetInterchange with systems that want 2026-03-28T23:30+01:00. No rules, so no surprises — and no DST.
DurationSeconds + nanos—Elapsed time: a timeout, a job's run time, "3 hours from now".
PeriodYears, months, days—Calendar distance: "10 working days", "one month's notice".

Rule of thumb: store an Instant, display a ZonedDateTime, schedule with a ZonedDateTime. A LocalDateTime in a database column is a bug waiting for the first user outside the server's zone.

Worked example

Spring 2026 in London: at 01:00 on Sunday 29 March the clocks jump to 02:00, so the hour 01:00–01:59 never happens. In October the reverse: 01:00–01:59 on the 25th happens twice. The program below places an order the evening before the spring change and then does the things people do to timestamps.

javaTimes.java
import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.time.Period;
import java.time.YearMonth;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import java.time.ZonedDateTime;
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.Locale;
 
public class Times {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ZoneId london = ZoneId.of("Europe/London");
 
        // an order placed the night before the clocks go forward (29 Mar 2026, 01:00 -> 02:00)
        ZonedDateTime placed = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 3, 28, 23, 30).atZone(london);
        System.out.println("placed            = " + placed);
        System.out.println("plusDays(1)       = " + placed.plusDays(1));     // same wall clock, 23h later
        System.out.println("plusHours(24)     = " + placed.plusHours(24));   // 24h later, different wall clock
 
        // a time that does not exist, and one that exists twice
        ZonedDateTime inGap = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 3, 29, 1, 30).atZone(london);
        System.out.println("01:30 in the gap  = " + inGap);
        ZonedDateTime overlap = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 25, 1, 30).atZone(london);
        System.out.println("01:30 in overlap  = " + overlap + " / later: " + overlap.withLaterOffsetAtOverlap());
 
        // one instant, three views
        Instant at = placed.toInstant();
        System.out.println("instant           = " + at);
        System.out.println("same instant NYC  = " + at.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York")));
        System.out.println("same instant Tokyo= " + at.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo")));
 
        // Period counts calendar units; Duration counts elapsed time
        LocalDate due = placed.toLocalDate().plusDays(10);
        System.out.println("SLA period        = " + Period.between(placed.toLocalDate(), due));
        System.out.println("elapsed to +1 day = " + Duration.between(placed, placed.plusDays(1)));
 
        // formatting: ISO is locale-free; a pattern needs a Locale
        DateTimeFormatter uk = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy HH:mm", Locale.UK);
        System.out.println("ISO_LOCAL_DATE    = " + placed.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE));
        System.out.println("pattern, UK       = " + placed.format(uk));
 
        // calendar arithmetic clamps rather than overflowing
        LocalDate jan31 = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31);
        System.out.println("31 Jan + 1 month  = " + jan31.plusMonths(1));
        System.out.println("truncated to hour = " + placed.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.HOURS).toLocalDateTime());
        YearMonth ym = YearMonth.from(placed);
        System.out.println("year-month        = " + ym + " (" + ym.lengthOfMonth() + " days)");
        System.out.println("day of week       = " + placed.getDayOfWeek() + ", weekend=" + (placed.getDayOfWeek() == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY));
        System.out.println("parsed + 1 week   = " + LocalDate.parse("2026-10-15").plusWeeks(1));
 
        // every java.time type is immutable: this line does nothing
        placed.plusDays(30);
        System.out.println("still placed on   = " + placed.toLocalDate());
    }
}
Expected output
placed            = 2026-03-28T23:30Z[Europe/London]
plusDays(1)       = 2026-03-29T23:30+01:00[Europe/London]
plusHours(24)     = 2026-03-30T00:30+01:00[Europe/London]
01:30 in the gap  = 2026-03-29T02:30+01:00[Europe/London]
01:30 in overlap  = 2026-10-25T01:30+01:00[Europe/London] / later: 2026-10-25T01:30Z[Europe/London]
instant           = 2026-03-28T23:30:00Z
same instant NYC  = 2026-03-28T19:30-04:00[America/New_York]
same instant Tokyo= 2026-03-29T08:30+09:00[Asia/Tokyo]
SLA period        = P10D
elapsed to +1 day = PT23H
ISO_LOCAL_DATE    = 2026-03-28
pattern, UK       = 28 Mar 2026 23:30
31 Jan + 1 month  = 2026-02-28
truncated to hour = 2026-03-28T23:00
year-month        = 2026-03 (31 days)
day of week       = SATURDAY, weekend=true
parsed + 1 week   = 2026-10-22
still placed on   = 2026-03-28

Read the first three lines together. plusDays(1) and plusHours(24) look interchangeable and are not: the first keeps the wall clock at 23:30 and lands on the 29th, only 23 real hours later, because the day it crossed had 23 hours. The second adds exactly 24 hours of elapsed time and lands at 00:30 on the 30th. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions. "Same time tomorrow" is a calendar question; "the 24-hour timeout expires" is an elapsed-time question. Pick the method that matches the question, not the one that reads most naturally.

The Z versus +01:00 at the end of each value is the offset java.time resolved from the zone rules at that instant. The zone (Europe/London) is stable; the offset is a consequence. That is also why the gap line prints 02:30: there was no 01:30, so the value was pushed forward by the length of the gap and given the post-change offset. In the overlap, 01:30 exists twice and the earlier one (still on summer time, +01:00) is chosen unless you ask for the later.

Try the arithmetic

Calendar versus elapsed, across the 2026 London clock changes Simulated

Computed in the browser from the same rules java.time applies to Europe/London in 2026 — clocks forward 29 March, back 25 October. Pick a start, an amount, and the kind of amount.

Period is a calendar, Duration is a stopwatch

A Period is years, months and days as fields — P10D above is "ten days", and P1M is "one month" whatever length that month turns out to have. A Duration is a count of seconds — PT23H — with no idea what a month is; Duration.ofDays(1) is sugar for 86,400 seconds. The consequence on a ZonedDateTime:

  • plus(Period), plusDays, plusMonths, plusYears work on the local date-time and then re-resolve the zone. Wall clock preserved; elapsed time varies.
  • plus(Duration), plusHours, plusMinutes, plusSeconds work on the instant. Elapsed time preserved; wall clock varies.

On a LocalDateTime there is no zone, so the two agree and plusDays(1) is always 24 hours. That is exactly why it is the wrong type for anything that will later be shown in a zone: the arithmetic is done before the question of "which 24 hours" can be asked.

Month arithmetic clamps. 31 January + 1 month is 28 February, and 28 February + 1 month is 28 March — so plusMonths(1).minusMonths(1) does not necessarily return where it started. If you need "same day next month or the last day if there is none", that is the behaviour you already have; if you need something else, say it explicitly with TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth().

ZoneId versus ZoneOffset

A ZoneId such as Europe/London names a set of rules maintained in the IANA tz database that the JDK ships and updates: which offset applies when, including every historical and scheduled DST change. A ZoneOffset such as +01:00 is a fixed number of seconds from UTC and knows nothing. A ZonedDateTime holds both — the id you gave it and the offset it derived — and re-derives the offset whenever the date-time changes. An OffsetDateTime holds only the offset, which is why adding a day to it never crosses a DST boundary: it cannot.

Use ZoneId.of("Europe/London"), never ZoneId.of("BST") or "GMT+1": the three-letter abbreviations are ambiguous (CST is three different zones) and a fixed offset silently stops being right in March. When you need the server's zone, ZoneId.systemDefault() exists — but code that depends on it behaves differently on every machine it runs on, which is the problem java.time was designed to let you avoid.

Formatting and parsing

Two families of formatter. The ISO constants (ISO_LOCAL_DATE, ISO_INSTANT, ISO_ZONED_DATE_TIME) are locale-independent, round-trip exactly, and are what toString() and parse(CharSequence) use; they are the right choice for anything machine-read. Pattern formatters from ofPattern are for humans, and a human has a locale: month names, day names, am/pm markers and even digits vary. Always pass one — ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy", Locale.UK) — because the overload without a locale uses the JVM default, and the same build will print Mar on one machine and mars on another.

The pattern letters are case-sensitive and the cases are traps. MM is month, mm is minute. HH is 0–23, hh is 1–12 and is meaningless without a. yyyy is the year of era, uuuu is the proleptic year (they differ only before year 1), and YYYY is the week-based year — the one that prints 2025 for 30 December 2024, because that Monday starts ISO week 1 of 2025. YYYY has appeared in more production date bugs than any other four characters; if you did not specifically want week numbering, you wanted yyyy.

Parsing is strict by default: LocalDate.parse("2026-2-3") throws DateTimeParseException because the ISO format requires two-digit months. That strictness is a feature — a lenient parser is how 31/02/2026 turns into 3 March without anyone noticing.

The legacy types, and testable time

java.util.Date is a mutable millisecond timestamp with a misleading name; Calendar is mutable, zero-indexes its months, and is not thread-safe. You will still meet them at the edges — JDBC drivers, old libraries, java.sql.Timestamp — so know the bridges and keep them at the boundary: date.toInstant() and Date.from(instant); calendar.toInstant(); timestamp.toLocalDateTime(). Convert on the way in, work in java.time, convert on the way out.

Code that calls Instant.now() or LocalDate.now() directly cannot be tested for "what happens at midnight" or "what happens during the DST overlap" without waiting for those moments. Every now() has an overload taking a Clock; inject one. In production, Clock.systemUTC(). In a test, Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-25T00:30:00Z"), ZoneId.of("Europe/London")), and the overlap is now a unit test that runs in a millisecond. That is also why every program in this module uses fixed dates: the output has to be the same on the day you read it as on the day it was built.

Five ways to get it wrong without an exception
  • Ignoring the return value. placed.plusDays(30); on its own does nothing — every java.time type is immutable, and the new value was discarded. The program above does exactly this on its highlighted last lines to prove it. Static analysis tools flag it; the compiler does not.
  • YYYY in a pattern. Week-based year. Correct for 51 weeks and wrong at the one moment nobody is watching.
  • Storing a LocalDateTime for an event. Without a zone it is not a point in time. Two servers in two zones will disagree about when it happened, and there is no way back to the truth.
  • Duration.ofDays(1) where you meant "tomorrow". It is 86,400 seconds. Twice a year, in every zone with DST, that is not one calendar day.
  • equals on ZonedDateTime. It compares the zone and the local fields, so the same instant viewed from London and Tokyo is not equal. Use isEqual, or compare the Instants.

Check yourself

1.A courier promise says "delivered within 24 hours of the order being placed". An order is placed at 23:30 on 28 March 2026 in London. Which expression gives the deadline, and when is it?

C. "Within 24 hours" is elapsed time, so it is a Duration question and plusHours(24) is the right tool. The night of 28–29 March has only 23 hours in London, so 24 real hours after 23:30 is 00:30 on the 30th.

A is what plusDays(1) really produces, but it is only 23 hours later — the courier would be judged against a deadline one hour too early. B and D each pair a method with the result the other method gives.

2.You are storing a customer's chosen delivery slot — "Tuesday 7 April 2027, 09:00, at their address in Madrid" — to be acted on next year. Which type should the field be?

B. A future appointment is a wall-clock promise in a place. If Spain changes its DST rules before April 2027 — governments do — a ZonedDateTime re-resolves to the new correct instant when the JDK's tz data is updated, and still means 09:00 on the customer's clock.

A freezes the instant under today's rules; after a rule change it would be an hour off and nothing would flag it. "Store instants" is the rule for things that have happened, not for promises about the future. C loses the zone entirely — "obvious from the address" is not something the type system can see, and the next developer will call atZone(systemDefault()). D hard-codes an offset that is only correct in summer; it is the fixed-offset mistake with a type to make it look deliberate.

3.What does LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 30).format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd", Locale.UK)) produce?

C. Upper-case Y is the week-based year. 30 December 2024 is a Monday, and under the UK's ISO week rules that Monday begins week 1 of 2025, so the year field prints 2025 while the month and day still print December 30. The result is a date that does not exist.

A is what yyyy prints and what the author meant. B: Y is perfectly valid, which is the whole problem. D: a pattern is a runtime string; the compiler has no opinion about its contents.

Section 13

Files, paths and I/O

Stock arrives as a CSV export, orders leave as a report, and both must survive a machine that was not the one you developed on. Java has two generations of file API. java.io (1996) is a family of streams — byte pipes and character pipes you wrap around each other. java.nio.file (Java 7) adds Path and Files: a model of the file system plus static helpers that do the common jobs in one call and open the right stream for you underneath. Use the second; understand the first, because it is what the second returns when the one-liner is not enough.

Path is a value, not a file

A Path is an immutable, parsed path string — segments plus a root — with no requirement that anything exists on disk. Every method below is pure string manipulation; only Files touches the file system. Given Path base = Path.of("data", "2026"):

Common Path operations with their results
ExpressionResultWhat it does
base.resolve("stock.csv")data/2026/stock.csvAppends a relative path. If the argument is absolute, the result is the argument — a classic surprise with user input.
base.resolveSibling("2027")data/2027Replaces the last segment.
base.relativize(Path.of("data/2026/archive/x.csv"))archive/x.csvThe path from base to the argument. Both must be relative or both absolute.
Path.of("data/./2026/../2026").normalize()data/2026Removes . and .. textually — it does not follow symlinks.
base.getFileName()2026The last segment, even when it is a directory.
base.getParent()datanull for a single-segment path — guard it.
base.toAbsolutePath()/home/…/data/2026Resolved against the JVM's working directory, which is wherever the process was started, not where the class file lives.
base.startsWith("data")trueSegment-wise, so Path.of("database") does not start with "data". Use it, not string startsWith, to check a path stays inside a directory.

On Windows the separator is \ and a root is C:\; on everything else it is /. Path.of("data", "stock.csv") with separate segments is correct everywhere; Path.of("data/stock.csv") happens to work on Windows too, but Path.of("data\\stock.csv") is a single file name on Linux.

Worked example

Write a small stock file, read it back three different ways, copy it into an archive, list what exists, and clean up. Everything happens in a fresh temporary directory, and only names relative to it are printed, so the output is identical on every machine.

javaFilesDemo.java
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
 
public class FilesDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("inventory-");   // somewhere under java.io.tmpdir
        Path csv = dir.resolve("stock.csv");
 
        Files.writeString(csv, """
                # sku,qty
                BOLT-7,10
                NUT-3,4
 
                CAM-9,2
                """, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        System.out.println("file             = " + csv.getFileName());
        System.out.println("size in bytes    = " + Files.size(csv));
 
        // 1. the whole file in memory
        List<String> all = Files.readAllLines(csv, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        System.out.println("readAllLines     = " + all.size() + " lines");
 
        // 2. a lazy stream - the file stays open until the try block ends
        long units;
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(csv, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            units = lines.map(String::strip)
                         .filter(l -> !l.isEmpty() && !l.startsWith("#"))
                         .mapToLong(l -> Long.parseLong(l.split(",")[1]))
                         .sum();
        }
        System.out.println("units via lines  = " + units);
 
        // 3. a buffered reader, one line at a time
        int skus = 0;
        try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(csv, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            String line;
            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {
                if (line.isBlank() || line.startsWith("#")) continue;
                skus++;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("skus via reader  = " + skus);
 
        // directories, copies, and a walk
        Path archive = Files.createDirectories(dir.resolve("archive"));
        Path copy = Files.copy(csv, archive.resolve("stock-2026-10-15.csv"), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
        System.out.println("copied to        = " + slashes(dir.relativize(copy)));
        try (Stream<Path> walk = Files.walk(dir)) {
            System.out.println("regular files    = " + walk.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
                    .map(p -> slashes(dir.relativize(p)))
                    .sorted()
                    .toList());
        }
        System.out.println("exists           = " + Files.exists(copy)
                + ", notExists(nope.csv) = " + Files.notExists(dir.resolve("nope.csv")));
 
        // a missing file is a specific IOException, not a null
        try {
            Files.readString(dir.resolve("nope.csv"));
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
            System.out.println("NoSuchFile       = " + Path.of(e.getFile()).getFileName());
        }
 
        // delete children before parents; a non-empty directory refuses
        Files.delete(copy);
        Files.delete(archive);
        Files.delete(csv);
        Files.delete(dir);
        System.out.println("cleaned up       = " + Files.notExists(dir));
    }
 
    // Windows separates with '\'; print '/' so the lesson reads the same everywhere
    static String slashes(Path p) { return p.toString().replace(p.getFileSystem().getSeparator(), "/"); }
}
Expected output
file             = stock.csv
size in bytes    = 37
readAllLines     = 5 lines
units via lines  = 16
skus via reader  = 3
copied to        = archive/stock-2026-10-15.csv
regular files    = [archive/stock-2026-10-15.csv, stock.csv]
exists           = true, notExists(nope.csv) = true
NoSuchFile       = nope.csv
cleaned up       = true

Thirty-seven bytes for five lines: the text block normalises every line ending to \n regardless of the platform the source was saved on, and UTF-8 encodes these ASCII characters one byte each. readAllLines gives five strings including the comment and the blank; the stream version filters both out and sums the quantities; the reader counts the SKUs. Three tools for three shapes of problem, and the choice between them is the subject of the next three subsections.

Notice what the walk returned: a sorted list of relative paths. Files.walk yields paths in file-system order, which is not specified and differs between NTFS and ext4, so a program that prints or compares them unsorted is non-deterministic. Also notice the order of the four delete calls. Files.delete on a directory that still has a file in it throws DirectoryNotEmptyException; children first, then parents.

Three layers, one file

// InputStream / OutputStream: raw bytes, no idea what a character is
try (InputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(Files.newInputStream(csv))) {
    byte[] header = in.readNBytes(9);          // "# sku,qty" as UTF-8 bytes
    int b;
    while ((b = in.read()) != -1) { /* one byte at a time, buffered underneath */ }
}
  • The bottom layer. Images, zips, sockets, anything binary.
  • read() returns an int 0–255, or −1 at end of stream — the int is so that −1 cannot collide with a byte value.
  • Unbuffered, every read() is a system call. Wrap in BufferedInputStream or read in chunks.
// Reader / Writer: characters, decoded from bytes by a Charset you choose
try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
        new InputStreamReader(Files.newInputStream(csv), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
    String line = in.readLine();               // null at end of stream
}
// ...which is exactly what Files.newBufferedReader(csv, UTF_8) builds for you
  • Text. InputStreamReader is the bridge: it decodes bytes into chars using the charset you pass.
  • BufferedReader adds the buffer and readLine(), which handles \n, \r\n and \r alike.
  • FileReader and FileWriter exist; before Java 11 they could not take a charset. Prefer the Files factories.
String whole      = Files.readString(csv, UTF_8);            // small text file
List<String> rows = Files.readAllLines(csv, UTF_8);          // small text file, by line
byte[] raw        = Files.readAllBytes(csv);                 // small binary file
try (Stream<String> s = Files.lines(csv, UTF_8)) { ... }     // any size, lazily
Files.writeString(out, text, UTF_8);                         // create or truncate
Files.write(out, rows, UTF_8, StandardOpenOption.APPEND);    // explicit options
  • Each helper opens the right stream, buffers it, and closes it — except lines and walk, which return a stream that you must close.
  • The readAll* family loads the entire file into memory. Fine for a config file; wrong for a 4 GB log.
  • Write options default to CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING, WRITE — a silent overwrite unless you say APPEND or CREATE_NEW.

Charsets: say what you mean

A file is bytes. Turning bytes into text requires a charset, and a charset is not a property of the file — nothing in stock.csv records that it was written as UTF-8. If the writer and the reader disagree, there is no exception: é written as the two UTF-8 bytes C3 A9 and read as ISO-8859-1 comes back as Ã©, and the first anyone hears of it is a customer complaint. Until Java 17 the no-argument overloads used the platform default, which was UTF-8 on Linux and windows-1252 on most Windows machines, so code passed its tests on the developer's laptop and corrupted data on the server. Java 18 (JEP 400) made UTF-8 the default everywhere, but the rule has not changed: pass the charset explicitly, because explicit is what a reader six months from now can verify.

Buffering, and why readLine is not expensive

A file system call costs microseconds; a Java method call costs nanoseconds. An unbuffered stream makes one system call per read(); a BufferedReader makes one per 8 KB and serves readLine() from memory. The difference on a hundred-megabyte file is seconds versus minutes. Every Files helper is buffered already. If you build a stream by hand, wrap it — and wrap the outermost layer you read from, so the buffer sits between you and the decoder, not between the decoder and the disk.

Lazy streams hold the file open

Files.lines and Files.walk are the two Files helpers that return a Stream. The stream reads on demand, which is what lets it handle a file bigger than memory — and it means the file descriptor stays open until the stream is closed. Stream implements AutoCloseable precisely for this: always put it in a try-with-resources, as the worked example does on its highlighted lines. Without that, the handle is released only when the garbage collector finalises the stream, which may be never; on Windows the file cannot be deleted or renamed in the meantime, and on any OS a loop that forgets this will eventually hit too many open files.

For a large file, Files.lines or newBufferedReader and a loop are the only options. readAllLines is simpler, and the right choice when the file is known to be small — but "known" means a config file you ship, not a CSV a customer uploads.

Tokenised input: Scanner

Scanner splits a source on whitespace (or a regex you supply) and parses tokens on demand: nextInt(), nextLine(), hasNext(). It is convenient for small structured input and for System.in. It has two traps. It is slow — it compiles regular expressions per token — so it is not for bulk files. And nextInt() leaves the line terminator unread, so a following nextLine() returns an empty string; the fix is an extra nextLine() to consume it, or reading whole lines and parsing them yourself, which is clearer anyway. Construct it as new Scanner(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) — the charset argument exists for the same reason as everywhere else.

The exceptions are specific

Subclasses of IOException thrown by java.nio.file and what each means
ExceptionThrown whenUsually fix by
NoSuchFileExceptionThe path does not existChecking the working directory — relative paths resolve from where the JVM was started.
FileAlreadyExistsExceptioncreateFile, createDirectory, or copy without REPLACE_EXISTING hits an existing targetDeciding deliberately: replace, append, or refuse.
AccessDeniedExceptionPermissions, or on Windows a file another process has openClosing the stream that still holds it.
DirectoryNotEmptyExceptiondelete on a directory with contentsWalking it depth-first and deleting children first.
NotDirectoryExceptionlist or newDirectoryStream on a regular fileChecking Files.isDirectory first.
MalformedInputExceptionBytes that are not valid in the charset you decoded withUsing the charset the file was actually written in.

All of these extend IOException, so a bare catch (IOException e) catches them all — and throws away the diagnosis. Catch the specific one when you can act on it (a missing optional config file is not an error; a missing required one is), and let the rest propagate with the message intact. Files.exists before readString does not replace this: the file can disappear between the two calls, and the check costs a system call that the read was going to make anyway.

For recursive operations, Files.walk plus a stream is usually enough; Files.walkFileTree with a FileVisitor is the heavier tool when you need to react to directories before and after their contents, or to continue past unreadable subtrees. And if an old API hands you a java.io.File, file.toPath() converts it, and path.toFile() goes back; do the conversion at the boundary and stay in java.nio.file.

Where file code goes wrong
  • Files.lines(path).count() with no try. Compiles, runs, leaks a file handle every call. The symptom shows up hours later as a failed delete or an exhausted descriptor table.
  • Relative paths and the working directory. Path.of("config.properties") resolves against the directory the JVM was launched from. It works from your IDE and fails from systemd. Resolve against a known base, or read from the classpath.
  • Files.write truncates by default. Writing a log line with the default options replaces the log. Pass StandardOpenOption.APPEND, and CREATE if the file may not exist.
  • Trusting resolve with user input. base.resolve(userSupplied) returns userSupplied unchanged if it is absolute, and .. segments walk out of base. Normalise, then check startsWith(base), before touching the disk.
  • readAllBytes on a file you did not size first. Arrays are limited to 231 elements and your heap is smaller than that. Stream anything that could be large.

Check yourself

1.On a Windows server, long n = Files.lines(report, UTF_8).count(); runs and returns the right number, but the scheduled job that then calls Files.delete(report) fails with AccessDeniedException. Why?

C. Files.lines opens the file and the returned Stream owns that handle; a terminal operation consumes the elements but does not close the stream. The handle is released when close() runs — which here is never, or whenever the garbage collector gets round to it. Windows enforces sharing locks, so an open file cannot be deleted; on Linux the delete would succeed and the leak would go unnoticed for longer.

A invents a state: a consumed stream is just a closed-for-reuse stream, not a lock, and the resource is released by close(), not by exit. B would fail every run, not only the ones after a count. D: lines uses an ordinary buffered reader, not a memory map, and even mapped files can be deleted on Linux.

2.A customer's export was written by a tool that uses windows-1252. Your import reads it with Files.readAllLines(p, StandardCharsets.UTF_8). The file contains a product called Écrou M8. What happens?

B. In windows-1252, É is the single byte C9. A UTF-8 decoder reads C9 as the start of a two-byte sequence and finds 63 (c) next, which is not a valid continuation byte. The Files helpers use a decoder configured to report malformed input, so you get an exception naming the position. That is the good outcome: the import stops instead of storing garbage.

A: nothing in a file declares its encoding and Java does not guess. C is what a hand-built InputStreamReader does — its decoder defaults to replacing bad input with U+FFFD, which is why the same bug in older code is silent. D confuses code points with bytes: the character is the same, the bytes are not.

3.An upload endpoint saves files as uploads.resolve(filename) where filename comes from the request. Which checks are needed to keep the write inside uploads? Select all that apply.

A and D. uploads.resolve("../../etc/passwd") is a legal path that normalize() turns into something outside uploads; the segment-wise startsWith check catches it. And uploads.resolve("/etc/passwd") is simply /etc/passwd — the documented behaviour for an absolute argument — so absolute input must be rejected before or by the same check. Simplest of all is to keep only Path.of(filename).getFileName(), which cannot contain a separator.

B is incomplete: on Windows \ is also a separator, and it does nothing about ... C is the assumption that makes directory-traversal bugs.

Put it together

Hands-on lab: the pricing and reporting pipeline

Six steps that turn the Fundamentals warehouse into a reporting system, each exercising something from this module. Write each step before opening its solution — the solutions are short, and reading one you have not attempted teaches almost nothing. The whole thing fits in one file; a real project would split the records, the discounts and the catalogue into their own.

Starter
mkdir order-lab && cd order-lab
# one file, OrderLab.java, grown step by step
javac OrderLab.java && java OrderLab

JDK 21 is required: record patterns in switch (step 2) were finalised in 21. Prices stay in cents as long — never double for money.

Step 1 — the domain as records §8

Define a Category enum and three records: Product(sku, name, category, priceInCents), OrderLine(product, qty) with a subtotal(), and Order(id, placed, lines) with a subtotal() that sums its lines. Validate in compact constructors: no blank SKU, no negative price, no non-positive quantity, no empty order. Make sure an Order cannot be changed by whoever still holds the list that was passed in.

Solution — step 1
enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MECHANICAL }
 
record Product(String sku, String name, Category category, long priceInCents) {
    Product {
        if (sku == null || sku.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku required");
        Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
        Objects.requireNonNull(category, "category");
        if (priceInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must not be negative: " + priceInCents);
    }
}
 
record OrderLine(Product product, int qty) {
    OrderLine {
        Objects.requireNonNull(product, "product");
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty);
    }
    long subtotal() { return product.priceInCents() * qty; }
}
 
record Order(String id, LocalDate placed, List<OrderLine> lines) {
    Order {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
        Objects.requireNonNull(placed, "placed");
        lines = List.copyOf(lines);                 // the record keeps its own immutable copy
        if (lines.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("order " + id + " has no lines");
    }
    long subtotal() { return lines.stream().mapToLong(OrderLine::subtotal).sum(); }
}

A compact constructor runs before the fields are assigned, so reassigning the parameter lines is how a record normalises its input. List.copyOf gives an immutable, null-rejecting copy — without it, the caller's ArrayList is still reachable and a record that looks immutable is not. equals, hashCode and toString come free and are component-wise, which step 3 relies on when products become map keys.

Step 2 — a sealed discount family §9

Model three discount kinds as a sealed interface Discount with record implementations: PercentOff(percent), FixedOff(cents) and BuyNGetOne(sku, n) ("buy n, get one free" for a single SKU). Write static long discountFor(Discount d, Order order) as a switch expression using record patterns, with no default branch. A fixed discount must never exceed the order's subtotal.

Solution — step 2
sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne {}
record PercentOff(int percent) implements Discount {
    PercentOff { if (percent < 0 || percent > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percent out of range: " + percent); }
}
record FixedOff(long cents) implements Discount {}
record BuyNGetOne(String sku, int n) implements Discount {}
 
static long discountFor(Discount d, Order order) {
    return switch (d) {
        case PercentOff(int pct)           -> order.subtotal() * pct / 100;
        case FixedOff(long cents)          -> Math.min(cents, order.subtotal());
        case BuyNGetOne(String sku, int n) -> order.lines().stream()
                .filter(l -> l.product().sku().equals(sku))
                .mapToLong(l -> (long) (l.qty() / (n + 1)) * l.product().priceInCents())
                .sum();
    };
}

Because the interface is sealed, the compiler knows the three cases are all the cases and accepts the switch without a default. That is the point: add a fourth discount next quarter and this method stops compiling until it handles it, instead of silently returning zero. A default would have thrown that guarantee away. The record patterns pull the components straight out — no accessor calls, no casts.

Step 3 — the report §5, §6

Given a List<Order>, produce three things with streams and collectors: revenue by Category as a TreeMap; the top three products by revenue as "SKU=cents" strings, ties broken by SKU; and a partition of order ids by whether the order's subtotal exceeds 10,000 cents. Every result must come out in a deterministic order.

Solution — step 3
Map<Category, Long> byCategory = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(l -> l.product().category(), TreeMap::new,
                                       Collectors.summingLong(OrderLine::subtotal)));
 
Map<String, Long> bySku = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(l -> l.product().sku(), Collectors.summingLong(OrderLine::subtotal)));
List<String> top3 = bySku.entrySet().stream()
        .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
        .limit(3)
        .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue())
        .toList();
 
Map<Boolean, List<String>> bigOrders = orders.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.subtotal() > 10_000,
                                           Collectors.mapping(Order::id, Collectors.toList())));

flatMap turns a stream of orders into a stream of lines, which is the grain the first two reports need. The three-argument groupingBy chooses the map type; a TreeMap keyed by an enum iterates in declaration order, so the category report is stable. The top-three query groups into a plain HashMap — order there is irrelevant because the next line sorts — and the explicit type witness on comparingByValue is needed because reversed() breaks the inference chain. partitioningBy always produces both keys, so a report never has to guess whether true is present.

Step 4 — lookups that cannot NPE §7

Write a Catalogue with void add(Product) and Optional<Product> findBySku(String). Then, without calling get() or isPresent(), obtain the price of CAM-9 (throwing IllegalStateException if absent) and the name of NOPE-0 with a fallback string.

Solution — step 4
static final class Catalogue {
    private final Map<String, Product> bySku = new HashMap<>();
    void add(Product p) { bySku.put(p.sku(), p); }
    Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku) { return Optional.ofNullable(bySku.get(sku)); }
}
 
long camPrice = catalogue.findBySku("CAM-9")
        .map(Product::priceInCents)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("CAM-9 not in catalogue"));
String unknown = catalogue.findBySku("NOPE-0").map(Product::name).orElse("(unknown sku)");

Optional.ofNullable is the bridge from a Map.get that returns null to an API that says so in its type. map carries the absence through, so the chain reads as the happy path and the fallback is stated once at the end. The exception supplier is a lambda so the message string is only built when it is needed; orElse is fine for a constant string but would be orElseGet if the fallback were expensive.

Step 5 — a composed ranking §10

Rank the orders by subtotal, highest first, and for equal subtotals by the date placed, earliest first. Produce "id(subtotal)" strings. Build the Comparator from the static factories, not a hand-written compare.

Solution — step 5
List<String> ranked = orders.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Order::subtotal).reversed().thenComparing(Order::placed))
        .map(o -> o.id() + "(" + o.subtotal() + ")")
        .toList();

comparingLong avoids boxing every subtotal; reversed() flips only the key before it, so the tiebreak that follows still runs ascending. LocalDate is Comparable, which is what lets thenComparing take the accessor directly. sorted is a stateful operation — it must see every order before it can emit the first — which is fine for a list of orders and worth knowing about for a stream of a million lines.

Step 6 — a time window §12

List the ids of orders placed in the seven days up to and including a reference date. Take the reference date as a parameter — LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 15) in main — rather than calling LocalDate.now(), so the method is testable and this page's output is reproducible.

Solution — step 6
LocalDate asOf = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 15);
LocalDate from = asOf.minusDays(7);
List<String> recent = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> !o.placed().isBefore(from))
        .map(Order::id)
        .toList();

!isBefore(from) is "on or after", the inclusive bound a window usually needs; isAfter(from) would silently drop orders placed exactly seven days ago. The reference date is a plain parameter here; in a service it would come from an injected Clock, which is the same idea with a type. Either way, "today" is an input, not something the method goes and fetches.

The finished thing

All six steps assembled. This program is compiled and executed during the build of this page, so the output below is what it really prints.

javaOrderLab.java
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
 
public class OrderLab {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MECHANICAL }
 
    // -- step 1: records with validating compact constructors -----------------
    record Product(String sku, String name, Category category, long priceInCents) {
        Product {
            if (sku == null || sku.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku required");
            Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
            Objects.requireNonNull(category, "category");
            if (priceInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("price must not be negative: " + priceInCents);
        }
    }
 
    record OrderLine(Product product, int qty) {
        OrderLine {
            Objects.requireNonNull(product, "product");
            if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive: " + qty);
        }
        long subtotal() { return product.priceInCents() * qty; }
    }
 
    record Order(String id, LocalDate placed, List<OrderLine> lines) {
        Order {
            Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id");
            Objects.requireNonNull(placed, "placed");
            lines = List.copyOf(lines);                       // immutable, null-hostile, ours
            if (lines.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("order " + id + " has no lines");
        }
        long subtotal() { return lines.stream().mapToLong(OrderLine::subtotal).sum(); }
    }
 
    // -- step 2: a sealed family consumed by an exhaustive switch -------------
    sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne {}
    record PercentOff(int percent) implements Discount {
        PercentOff { if (percent < 0 || percent > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("percent out of range: " + percent); }
    }
    record FixedOff(long cents) implements Discount {}
    record BuyNGetOne(String sku, int n) implements Discount {}
 
    static long discountFor(Discount d, Order order) {
        return switch (d) {                                   // no default: the compiler checks coverage
            case PercentOff(int pct)           -> order.subtotal() * pct / 100;
            case FixedOff(long cents)          -> Math.min(cents, order.subtotal());
            case BuyNGetOne(String sku, int n) -> order.lines().stream()
                    .filter(l -> l.product().sku().equals(sku))
                    .mapToLong(l -> (long) (l.qty() / (n + 1)) * l.product().priceInCents())
                    .sum();
        };
    }
 
    // -- step 4: an Optional-returning lookup ---------------------------------
    static final class Catalogue {
        private final Map<String, Product> bySku = new HashMap<>();
        void add(Product p) { bySku.put(p.sku(), p); }
        Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku) { return Optional.ofNullable(bySku.get(sku)); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Product bolt   = new Product("BOLT-7", "M8 bolt",      Category.FASTENER,   80);
        Product nut    = new Product("NUT-3",  "M8 nut",       Category.FASTENER,   25);
        Product girder = new Product("GIRD-1", "Steel girder", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000);
        Product cam    = new Product("CAM-9",  "Cam follower", Category.MECHANICAL, 1_450);
 
        Catalogue catalogue = new Catalogue();
        for (Product p : List.of(bolt, nut, girder, cam)) catalogue.add(p);
 
        List<Order> orders = List.of(
            new Order("A-100", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1),  List.of(new OrderLine(bolt, 40), new OrderLine(nut, 40))),
            new Order("A-101", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 9),  List.of(new OrderLine(girder, 1))),
            new Order("A-102", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 12), List.of(new OrderLine(cam, 6), new OrderLine(bolt, 10))),
            new Order("A-103", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 14), List.of(new OrderLine(cam, 2))));
 
        // step 2 in action
        Order a100 = orders.get(0);
        System.out.println("A-100 subtotal        = " + a100.subtotal());
        for (Discount d : List.of(new PercentOff(10), new FixedOff(5_000), new BuyNGetOne("BOLT-7", 3))) {
            System.out.printf("  %-27s -> %d off%n", d, discountFor(d, a100));
        }
 
        // -- step 3: the report -------------------------------------------------
        Map<Category, Long> byCategory = orders.stream()
                .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(l -> l.product().category(), TreeMap::new,
                                               Collectors.summingLong(OrderLine::subtotal)));
        System.out.println("revenue by category   = " + byCategory);
 
        Map<String, Long> bySku = orders.stream()
                .flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(l -> l.product().sku(), Collectors.summingLong(OrderLine::subtotal)));
        List<String> top3 = bySku.entrySet().stream()
                .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
                .limit(3)
                .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue())
                .toList();
        System.out.println("top 3 products        = " + top3);
 
        Map<Boolean, List<String>> bigOrders = orders.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.subtotal() > 10_000,
                                                   Collectors.mapping(Order::id, Collectors.toList())));
        System.out.println("over 10,000 cents     = " + bigOrders);
 
        // -- step 4: Optional without get() -------------------------------------
        long camPrice = catalogue.findBySku("CAM-9")
                .map(Product::priceInCents)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("CAM-9 not in catalogue"));
        String unknown = catalogue.findBySku("NOPE-0").map(Product::name).orElse("(unknown sku)");
        System.out.println("CAM-9 price           = " + camPrice + ", NOPE-0 -> " + unknown);
 
        // -- step 5: ranking with a composed Comparator -------------------------
        List<String> ranked = orders.stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Order::subtotal).reversed().thenComparing(Order::placed))
                .map(o -> o.id() + "(" + o.subtotal() + ")")
                .toList();
        System.out.println("ranked by total       = " + ranked);
 
        // -- step 6: a time window against a fixed reference date ---------------
        LocalDate asOf = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 15);
        LocalDate from = asOf.minusDays(7);
        List<String> recent = orders.stream()
                .filter(o -> !o.placed().isBefore(from))
                .map(Order::id)
                .toList();
        System.out.println("placed since " + from + " = " + recent);
    }
}
Expected output
A-100 subtotal        = 4200
  PercentOff[percent=10]      -> 420 off
  FixedOff[cents=5000]        -> 4200 off
  BuyNGetOne[sku=BOLT-7, n=3] -> 800 off
revenue by category   = {FASTENER=5000, STRUCTURAL=120000, MECHANICAL=11600}
top 3 products        = [GIRD-1=120000, CAM-9=11600, BOLT-7=4000]
over 10,000 cents     = {false=[A-100, A-102, A-103], true=[A-101]}
CAM-9 price           = 1450, NOPE-0 -> (unknown sku)
ranked by total       = [A-101(120000), A-102(9500), A-100(4200), A-103(2900)]
placed since 2026-10-08 = [A-101, A-102, A-103]

Two details in the output are worth a second look. The TreeMap lists STRUCTURAL before MECHANICAL — an enum's natural order is its declaration order, not alphabetical, which is exactly what a report usually wants and occasionally surprises. And the three discount lines are the record toString implementations, generated from the component names; a hand-written class would have needed three methods to print as clearly.

Extensions worth attempting
  • Add a fourth discount, FreeShippingOver(long threshold), to the sealed interface and do nothing else. Read the compiler error carefully — it is telling you every switch that now needs a case. Then add a Discount that is itself a record of two discounts applied in sequence; what does the pattern look like?
  • Load the orders from a CSV file with Files.lines (§13) instead of constructing them in main. Decide what a malformed line should do to the import: skip it, stop, or collect the failures with partitioningBy and report them at the end.
  • Replace the Catalogue's HashMap with a map keyed by Product itself, then change a product's price by creating a new Product record. Explain, before running it, why the old entry is still there — and why that is the correct behaviour for a value type.

Cheat sheet

Everything worth having in front of you while you write. This section is laid out to print cleanly — controls and navigation are hidden, and tables are kept whole across page breaks. Each block names the section it condenses.

Wildcards: the PECS decision §1

Which wildcard to use for a method parameter
The method…Parameter typeInside the methodCallers may pass

Wildcards go in parameters, never return types. Erasure forbids new T(), new T[n], instanceof List<String>, List<int>, static T, catch (T e), and two overloads that differ only by type argument.

Records §8

  • Header = complete state. Generated: private final fields, canonical constructor, name() accessors, equals, hashCode, toString.
  • Compact constructor Line { sku = sku.strip(); if (qty <= 0) throw …; }: validate and normalise the parameters; fields are assigned after the body. Other constructors must delegate with this(…).
  • Implicitly final; no extends; may implements; no instance fields beyond components; nested records are static; local records cannot capture locals.
  • Immutability is shallow: copy collection components with List.copyOf in the compact constructor; arrays break equals — use a List.
  • Not a record: anything with identity, anything that mutates, anything that needs a superclass or a no-arg constructor.

Sealed types and pattern switch §9

sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, BuyNGetOne {}
record PercentOff(int pct) implements Discount {}
record FixedOff(int cents) implements Discount {}
record BuyNGetOne(int n) implements Discount {}
 
long apply(Discount d, long gross, int qty) {
    return switch (d) {                                         // expression: must be exhaustive
        case null                       -> gross;               // without this, null throws NPE
        case FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross -> 0;              // guarded case first…
        case FixedOff(int c)            -> gross - c;           // …then the unguarded one
        case PercentOff(int pct)        -> gross * (100 - pct) / 100;
        case BuyNGetOne(int n)          -> { long free = qty / (n + 1); yield gross - free * (gross / qty); }
    };                                                          // no default: a new subtype is a compile error
}
Pattern forms
PatternExampleRule
Typecase String s ->specific before general, or "dominated by a preceding case label"
Recordcase FixedOff(int c) ->binds components by position; accessors run during matching
Nested recordcase Line(Product(var sku, var p), int qty) ->var infers each component
Guardcase FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross ->a guard is not a case: an unguarded one is still required
Nullcase null -> / case null, default ->otherwise a null selector throws
instanceofif (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3)binding is in scope wherever the test must have passed

Permitted subtypes must be final, sealed or non-sealed, in the same package or module. Exhaustiveness is checkable only for enums and sealed types. Sealed switch when types are fixed and operations grow; polymorphism when operations are fixed and types grow.

Integer.compare(a, b), never a - b. compareTo == 0 should mean equals: a TreeSet uses only the comparator and drops "equal" elements. Object sorts are stable TimSort; Arrays.sort(int[]) is dual-pivot quicksort.
