Rehearsal

Interview questions

Twelve questions that actually get asked about this material, with the answer a strong candidate gives. Say your answer out loud before opening the reveal — recognising an answer and being able to produce one are different skills.

Easy  1. What does PECS stand for, and how do you apply it?

Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Look at what the method does with the collection parameter. If it only reads elements out, the collection is a producer and the parameter should be List<? extends T>, so callers can pass a list of any subtype; inside, you may read as T but the compiler forbids add. If it only writes elements in, it is a consumer and should be List<? super T>, so a list of any supertype — even List<Object> — is accepted; inside, you may add a T but read only as Object. If it does both, no wildcard: the exact type, or a generic method <T>. The JDK's own Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the canonical example, and Comparable<? super T> in every sort signature is the same rule — the comparator consumes a T.

Easy  2. Why is a List<Integer> not a List<Number>, when an Integer is a Number?

Because if it were, you could write List<Number> nums = integers; nums.add(2.5); and put a Double into a list that other code still believes holds only Integers. The failure would appear later, as a ClassCastException at some unrelated get. Generic types are therefore invariant: List<A> and List<B> are unrelated however A and B relate. Arrays made the opposite choice — Integer[] is a Number[] — and pay for it with ArrayStoreException at runtime, which the generics designers regarded as a mistake not to repeat. The way to get the flexibility back safely is a wildcard: List<? extends Number> accepts the List<Integer> and, in exchange, forbids add.

Easy  3. What is the difference between a lambda and an anonymous inner class?

A lambda can only implement a functional interface — one abstract method — and has no identity of its own: this inside it is the enclosing instance, it cannot shadow a local, it introduces no new scope for names, and the compiler may reuse one instance for a non-capturing lambda. An anonymous class is a real class: it can implement several methods or extend a class, this is the anonymous object, it can have fields and shadow outer names, and every evaluation allocates a new object that holds a hidden reference to the enclosing instance. Both capture locals by copy and both require captured locals to be effectively final. The practical consequence: an IDE's "convert to lambda" silently changes the meaning of this and of any unqualified call to an inherited method, so a body that uses either must be reviewed, not just converted.

Easy  4. When would you use a record instead of a class, and what does "shallow immutability" mean?

A record is for a transparent carrier of immutable data: a value with no identity, equal when its components are equal, never changed after construction — DTOs, map keys, multi-value returns, stream intermediates. The compiler derives fields, canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from the header, and a compact constructor lets you validate and normalise before the automatic assignment runs. It is the wrong tool for anything with identity (a customer whose name changes is the same customer), anything that mutates, or anything that needs a superclass or a no-argument constructor. "Shallow" means the record's references are final but the objects behind them are whatever you passed: a List component can still be mutated by whoever holds the original. The idiom is lines = List.copyOf(lines); in the compact constructor, and a List rather than an array, since the generated equals compares arrays by identity.

Medium  5. A class inherits two default methods with the same signature. Which one runs?

Three rules, applied in order. First, a class wins over any interface: if a superclass anywhere up the chain has a concrete method with that signature, every interface default is ignored — this is what guarantees that adding a default to an interface cannot change what existing class hierarchies do. Second, a more specific interface wins: if Fragile extends Shippable and both define describe(), Fragile's body is chosen regardless of declaration order. Third, if the two interfaces are unrelated, the class must override the method itself or the compiler rejects it with "inherits unrelated defaults". Inside that override you may delegate to one with Shippable.super.describe(), the only place that syntax is legal. A follow-up they often add: a default cannot override an Object method such as toString, because rule one would make it pointless and the language forbids it outright.

Medium  6. What does laziness buy a stream pipeline, and which operations break it?

Nothing runs until a terminal operation asks for a result; then elements are pulled one at a time through the whole chain, vertically rather than stage by stage. That buys three things: short-circuiting (findFirst or limit can stop after examining two of a million elements), the ability to process sources bigger than memory or infinite (Files.lines, Stream.iterate), and fusion — filter and map run in a single pass with no intermediate collections. Stateful operations break it: sorted cannot emit its first element until it has seen the last, so it is a barrier that drains everything upstream and buffers it, and distinct must remember what it has seen. Put filter before sorted to give it less to drain. Two related points worth volunteering: a pipeline with no terminal operation is a silent no-op, and a stream is single-use — a second terminal throws IllegalStateException.

Medium  7. groupingBy versus partitioningBy — and what happens when toMap sees a duplicate key?

groupingBy(classifier, downstream) buckets elements by any key and applies a downstream collector to each bucket; keys appear only for values that actually occurred, so a lookup for an absent bucket returns null. partitioningBy(predicate, downstream) is the boolean special case with one extra guarantee: both true and false keys are always present, even when one side is empty. That guarantee is the only reason to prefer it, and it removes a null check. The two-argument toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key … the moment a second element maps to an existing key — it refuses to pick a winner silently, which is deliberate. Supply the three-argument form with a merge function — Integer::sum, Math::min, (a, b) -> a — to say what should happen, and the four-argument form with a map supplier if you need TreeMap or LinkedHashMap order. Also worth knowing: toMap rejects null values, unlike HashMap.put, and counting() returns Long.

Medium  8. Where should Optional be used, and where is it misused?

Its designers intended one use: a return type that says "this may be absent" so loudly the caller cannot forget. The right way to consume one is the chain — map, flatMap, filter, then orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow or ifPresentOrElse — so the question "and if empty?" is answered once, at the end. The misuses: get(), which is orElseThrow with a friendlier name, and isPresent() followed by get(), which is a null check in costume. As a field it is not Serializable, doubles the memory of every nullable field, and can itself still be null; as a parameter it forces every caller to wrap and the method must still guard against a null argument; as a collection element or wrapper around a collection it creates two ways to say "nothing". One performance trap: orElse(expensive()) evaluates its argument eagerly, present or not — use orElseGet for anything that does work. And never return null from a method typed Optional.

Medium  9. What does "consistent with equals" mean for a comparator, and what goes wrong without it?

The Comparable contract recommends that compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals returns true. It is not enforced, and the sorted collections are where the gap shows: TreeSet and TreeMap have no hash table and never call equals or hashCode — their only notion of "same element" is a comparison result of 0. Build a TreeSet with comparingInt(Product::priceInCents), add four products of which two cost 80, and the set silently holds three. The same input in a HashSet holds four. BigDecimal is the famous JDK case: 1.0 and 1.00 compare as 0 but are not equals. The fix is a tie-breaker that only returns 0 for genuinely equal elements — comparingInt(price).thenComparing(sku) — or a list instead of a set if duplicates by price are fine. Two more comparator points interviewers like: a - b overflows where Integer.compare does not, and reversed() reverses the whole chain built so far, not the last key.

Hard  10. When would you choose a sealed type with a pattern switch over ordinary polymorphism?

They solve opposite halves of the expression problem — no single design makes both adding types and adding operations cheap. Polymorphism puts each operation as a method on each type; adding a type is one new class and nothing else changes, but adding an operation touches every class. A sealed hierarchy with pattern switches puts each operation in one place with a case per type; adding an operation is one new method, and adding a type is a compile error at every switch that must now handle it — because a switch expression over a sealed type must be exhaustive and the compiler knows the complete set of permitted subtypes. So: sealed switch when the types are fixed and the operations keep growing (discount kinds, AST nodes, messages), polymorphism when the operations are fixed and the types keep growing (shapes in a drawing app). The one rule that makes the sealed version safe is to write no default: a default does not add safety, it removes it, by letting the new subtype fall silently into the fallback path in production. Record patterns and guards (when) let each case deconstruct and qualify in one line, and case null is needed because a pattern switch throws on null.

Hard  11. What does a HashMap do when it resizes, and why is a mutable key fatal?

The table is an array of bins whose length is a power of two; a key's bin is (length − 1) & hash, after spreading the hash with h ^ (h >>> 16) so the mask sees the high bits too. The map tracks a threshold of capacity × load factor, 16 × 0.75 = 12 by default; when the entry count exceeds it, the table doubles and every entry is re-inserted into its new bin. That rehash is O(n), but doublings are geometric so put stays amortised O(1); pre-sizing with the expected count divided by 0.75 skips every resize. Two consequences to volunteer: iteration order changes on resize, so code that happened to see insertion order breaks past 12 entries; and a bin that reaches 8 entries in a table of at least 64 bins becomes a red-black tree, which is the JDK defending against a bad hashCode. A mutable key breaks the structure because the entry sits in the bin chosen for its original hash: after mutation, a lookup by the new value goes to a different bin, a lookup by the old value reaches the right bin but fails equals, and even the original key object cannot find its own entry. Nothing throws; the entry is simply unreachable — until a resize happens to move it, at which point behaviour depends on how many other entries exist. Keys must be immutable: strings, records, boxed primitives.

Hard  12. How does daylight-saving time break date arithmetic, and why do you store Instants?

A point on the timeline and a reading on a wall clock are different things, and the mapping between them depends on a zone whose rules change twice a year. In London on 29 March 2026 the hour 01:00–01:59 does not exist; on 25 October it happens twice. So placed.plusDays(1) on a ZonedDateTime keeps the wall clock at 23:30 and lands only 23 real hours later, while plusHours(24) adds elapsed time and lands at 00:30 the day after. Neither is wrong — "same time tomorrow" is a Period question, "the 24-hour deadline" is a Duration question — and choosing the method that matches the question is the whole skill. A LocalDateTime cannot ask the question at all, because without a zone it is not a point in time: two servers in two zones will disagree about when it happened. So for anything that has happened you store an Instant, which is UTC and unambiguous, and convert to a ZonedDateTime with a region id like Europe/London — never a fixed offset or a three-letter abbreviation — only to display. For a future appointment you store the ZonedDateTime instead, because the customer means 09:00 on their clock even if the rules change before then. And inject a Clock, so the overlap is a unit test rather than a 2 a.m. incident in October.

Assessment

Self-assessment quiz

Sixteen questions covering all twelve learning objectives. Answer every one, then submit — nothing is marked until you do, and the explanations stay hidden until then. Your answers are saved locally, so you can leave and come back.

1.A method restock(List<…> dst) adds three Perishable objects to dst and reads nothing back. Which parameter type accepts the most callers while still compiling?

B. The method only writes, so the list is a consumer and Consumer Super applies: any list that a Perishable fits in — List<Perishable>, List<Product>, even List<Object> — is accepted, and add(Perishable) compiles inside. A is the producer form: it would accept a List<Milk> and then forbid add, because a Perishable is not necessarily a Milk. C forbids adding anything but null. D compiles but accepts only the exact type, rejecting a perfectly safe List<Product>.

2.Which of these are rejected by the compiler as a direct consequence of type erasure? Select all that apply.

A, B and D. After erasure the method body sees T as Object and has no class to construct (A); every List is the same runtime class so there is nothing for instanceof to test (B); and both overloads erase to f(List), the "same erasure" error (D). C is legal and ordinary — an unbounded wildcard accepts any parameterisation; it is the typed, safe alternative to a raw List.

3.class Order { class Cursor { } } — from a static void main in another class you write Order.Cursor c = new Order.Cursor();. What happens?

C. A nested class without static is inner: every instance carries a hidden this$0 reference to an Order, passed as a secret constructor argument, so it cannot be created without one. Either construct it through an instance — order.new Cursor(), or more usually a method on Order — or, if it never uses the outer instance, make it static. A describes what a static nested class would allow. B invents a rule; nothing is implicit. D cannot happen because the compiler refuses first.

4.int n = 0; Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(n); n = 1; r.run(); — what happens?

D. A lambda copies the value of a captured local, so a later assignment would leave two copies that disagree; the language forbids the situation rather than pick a meaning. The rule is checked per variable, not per use — one assignment anywhere in the method makes n uncapturable — and the error is reported at the capture, not at the assignment, which is why C has the location wrong. A is what would happen if the rule did not exist, and is exactly the surprise it prevents. B describes closures in languages that share variables; Java's do not.

5.class Base { public String describe() { return "base"; } }, interface Priced { default String describe() { return "priced"; } }, class Bolt extends Base implements Priced { }. What does new Bolt().describe() return?

A. Rule one of default resolution: a concrete method from a superclass, however far up, wins over every interface default. This is what makes defaults safe to add to published interfaces — they cannot change what an existing class hierarchy does. B applies the "more specific" rule to the wrong pair; that rule only ranks interfaces against each other. C is the outcome only when two unrelated interfaces supply the default and no class does. D: declaration order never affects resolution.

6.Predict the output:

String prefix = "SKU-";
Function<String, String> f = prefix::concat;
prefix = "PART-";       // compiles: prefix is reassigned, but the reference was already built
System.out.println(f.apply("7"));

A. prefix::concat is a bound instance reference: the receiver expression is evaluated once, when the reference is created, and the resulting Function holds that String object. Reassigning the variable afterwards changes nothing the function can see. The call is "SKU-".concat("7"). B would require the reference to re-read the variable at call time, which only a lambda s -> prefix.concat(s) would do — and that lambda would not compile, for the reason in D. D is wrong here because a bound method reference evaluates its receiver immediately and does not capture the variable; the effectively-final rule applies to lambdas and to references whose receiver is a captured local inside a lambda body, not to this form. C has the receiver and argument swapped — that is what the unbound String::concat applied as (a, b) -> a.concat(b) might suggest, but this reference is bound.

7.Predict the output:

List.of("a", "bb", "ccc").stream()
    .peek(s -> System.out.print(s + " "))
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 1)
    .findFirst();

B. findFirst is a terminal operation, so the pipeline runs — vertically, one element at a time. "a" is peeked, fails the filter, and the next element is pulled; "bb" is peeked, passes, and reaches findFirst, which has what it needs and stops. "ccc" is never read. A is what toList() would print, since it consumes everything. C forgets that peek runs before the filter and sees the rejected element too. D: discarding the result does not undo the terminal operation; only a pipeline with no terminal at all is a no-op.

8.Which intermediate operation must receive every upstream element before it can emit its first one?

B. The smallest element might be the last one in, so sorted is a barrier: it buffers the whole upstream, then emits in order. A limit placed after it still has to wait, and the buffer costs memory proportional to the input. A and D are stateless — each element is handled alone and passed on immediately. C is the opposite of a barrier: it is short-circuiting, and stops the upstream early.

9.The stream holds two FASTENER products. What does stock.stream().collect(toMap(Product::category, Product::sku)) do?

C. The two-argument toMap refuses to choose a winner: a second value for an existing key throws, naming the key and both values. That is deliberate, because silently keeping one would hide a data problem. To say what should happen, use the three-argument form — (a, b) -> b for A's behaviour, (a, b) -> a for B's, Integer::sum to total. D is wrong: the two-argument overload exists and compiles; the failure is at runtime.

10.What is the type of stock.stream().collect(groupingBy(Product::category, counting()))?

B. The downstream collector decides the value type, and counting() always produces Long. Declaring the result as Map<Category, Integer> (A) is the single most common compile error with groupingBy; use summingInt(p -> 1) if you genuinely need an Integer. C is the one-argument groupingBy, whose implicit downstream is toList(). D: the two-argument form promises a Map backed by a HashMap; a TreeMap needs the three-argument form with TreeMap::new as the middle argument.

11.In which of these positions should Optional not appear, according to its designers? Select all that apply.

A, B and C. A field (A) is not Serializable, doubles the memory of every nullable field, and can itself still be null; expose a nullable field through an accessor that returns Optional instead. A parameter (B) forces every caller to wrap, and the method must still guard against a null argument — two overloads are the idiom. A map value (C) gives Map.get two ways to say "nothing": null for an absent key and Optional.empty() for a present one. D is the one intended use: a return type that says "may be absent" so the caller cannot forget.

12.Predict the output:

record Line(String sku, int qty) {
    Line {
        sku = sku.strip().toUpperCase();
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty");
    }
}
System.out.println(new Line("  bolt-7 ", 2).equals(new Line("BOLT-7", 2)));

A. In a compact constructor the body runs before the compiler's automatic this.sku = sku; this.qty = qty;, so reassigning the parameter is exactly how you normalise: both records end up with the field "BOLT-7", and the generated equals compares fields, not the arguments that were passed. B and D both misdescribe the generated equals — it is component-wise, on the stored values. C is backwards: assigning this.sku in a compact constructor is the compile error, because the field is assigned for you afterwards.

13.sealed interface Discount permits PercentOff, FixedOff, both records. Does this compile?

long apply(Discount d, long gross) {
    return switch (d) {
        case PercentOff(int pct)                 -> gross * (100 - pct) / 100;
        case FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross     -> 0;
    };
}

C. A guard is not a case. case FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross handles only the vouchers worth more than the line; the compiler cannot prove anything about the rest, so the switch is not exhaustive and the error names FixedOff — the type you thought you had handled. Add an unguarded case FixedOff(int c) -> gross - c after it. A counts case labels instead of coverage. B describes separate-compilation drift, not a program the compiler has just seen. D is the opposite of the design: exhaustiveness without default is the whole point of sealing, and a default would hide the next subtype.

14.Predict the output:

List<String> src  = new ArrayList<>(List.of("BOLT-7"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(src);
src.add("NUT-3");
System.out.println(view.size() + " " + copy.size());

B. The view stores no elements; it forwards every read to src, so it sees the second element the moment it is added. The copy walked src once and owns its own storage, fixed at that instant. "Unmodifiable" describes the window, not the room. A treats the view as a snapshot; C treats the copy as a view. D: a view only refuses writes made through itself; the original list is unaffected by having been wrapped.

15.London's clocks go forward at 01:00 on 29 March 2026. Predict the output:

ZonedDateTime placed = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 28, 23, 30, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("Europe/London"));
System.out.println(Duration.between(placed, placed.plusDays(1)).toHours());

A. plusDays is calendar arithmetic on a ZonedDateTime: it keeps the wall clock at 23:30 and re-resolves the offset, so the result is 23:30 on the 29th — and because the night in between lost an hour, that is 23 real hours later. Duration.between measures elapsed time and reports it honestly. B is what plusHours(24) would give, landing at 00:30 on the 30th; it is also what a LocalDateTime would always say, having no zone to consult. C is the October overlap, not the March gap. D: 23:30 exists on both days; only 01:00–01:59 on the 29th is missing, and even a time in the gap is shifted forward rather than rejected.

16.Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); — which of these guarantee the file handle it opened is released? Select all that apply.

A and C. Files.lines reads on demand, so the returned stream owns an open file descriptor until close() runs; Stream implements AutoCloseable for exactly this reason, and try-with-resources is the idiom. B is the trap: a terminal operation consumes the elements and marks the stream as used, but does not close it — on Windows the file then cannot be deleted, and on Linux the descriptor leaks silently. D relies on the garbage collector finalising the stream, which may happen hours later or never. The same applies to Files.walk and Files.list.

Reference

Glossary

Thirty terms, each linked back to the section that introduces it. The same entries drive the flashcard deck below — one list, two ways to use it.

Flashcards

Bounded type parameter
<T extends Product>: a type variable that may only be instantiated with a subtype of the bound, which is what lets the method call Product's methods on a T. An intersection bound T extends Product & Stockable requires both. §1
Charset
The mapping between bytes and characters. A file does not record which one it was written with, so reading with the wrong charset throws MalformedInputException or produces Ã© for é. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly. §13
Collector
The recipe collect uses to accumulate a stream into a result: how to create a container, add an element, merge two containers and finish. Collectors supplies every common one — toList, toMap, groupingBy, joining, counting. §6
Compact constructor
A record constructor written without a parameter list — Line { sku = sku.strip(); } — whose body runs before the compiler's automatic field assignment. The place to validate and normalise; assigning this.x inside it is a compile error. §8
Comparator
An ordering supplied from outside the class, built with comparing, thenComparing, reversed and nullsFirst. Should return 0 only for elements that are equals, because TreeSet uses nothing else to detect duplicates. §10
Default method
An interface method with a body that implementers inherit unless they override it. Resolved by three rules: a class wins over an interface, a more specific interface wins over a less specific one, otherwise the class must override. Cannot override an Object method. §3
Defensive copy
Copying a mutable argument on the way into a class (new ArrayList<>(list), List.copyOf) and copying or wrapping on the way out, so no caller can reach the internal state. Rule two of an immutable class. §10
Downstream collector
The second collector handed to groupingBy or partitioningBy, applied to the elements inside each bucket: groupingBy(Product::category, summingLong(Product::value)). mapping, filtering and collectingAndThen adapt it. §6
DST gap
The hour that does not exist when clocks go forward — 01:00–01:59 in London on 29 March 2026. A ZonedDateTime placed in it is shifted forward by the gap's length; a day crossing it has 23 hours. The overlap in October is the hour that happens twice. §12
Duration versus Period
A Duration is elapsed seconds — a stopwatch — and moves the instant. A Period is calendar fields (years, months, days) and moves the wall clock. plusHours(24) and plusDays(1) differ by an hour across a DST change. §12
Effectively final
A local variable that is assigned exactly once and never changed, whether or not it is declared final. Only such locals may be captured by a lambda or inner class, because capture copies the value and a later write would leave two copies that disagree. §2
Erasure
The compiler checks generic type arguments and then drops them: bytecode holds a plain List and a checkcast at every read. Why new T(), new T[n], instanceof List<String>, List<int> and overloads differing only by type argument are all impossible. §1
Exhaustiveness
The compiler's proof that a switch expression handles every possible value of its selector. Checkable only for enums and sealed types, where the complete set is known; a default satisfies it but hides any subtype added later. §9
Fail-fast iterator
An iterator that remembers the collection's modCount at creation and throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next next() after any structural change it did not make. No threads needed. Remove safely with Iterator.remove or removeIf. §11
Functional interface
An interface with exactly one abstract method (defaults and statics do not count), which is what a lambda or method reference implements. Function, Predicate, Supplier, Consumer, Comparator, Runnable. @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce it. §4
Guard
A when clause on a switch case — case FixedOff(int c) when c >= gross — that restricts the pattern to values satisfying a condition. A guarded case covers only some values of its type, so an unguarded case for that type is still required. §9
Inner class
A nested class declared without static. Every instance holds a hidden this$0 reference to the enclosing instance, so it can only be created through one (order.new Cursor()) and keeps the outer object alive. If it does not use the outer instance, make it static. §2
Instant
A point on the timeline, measured in nanoseconds from 1970-01-01T00:00Z, with no zone and no ambiguity. The type to store and log for anything that has happened; convert to a ZonedDateTime only to display. §12
Lazy evaluation
Nothing in a stream pipeline runs until a terminal operation pulls, and then elements flow one at a time through every stage. Buys short-circuiting and the ability to process sources larger than memory; a pipeline with no terminal is a silent no-op. §5
Load factor
The fill ratio at which a HashMap doubles its table and rehashes every entry: 0.75 by default, so a 16-bin map resizes on its 13th entry. Iteration order changes at each resize; a bin reaching 8 entries in a table of 64 or more becomes a tree. §11
Method reference
Shorthand for a lambda whose body is one call forwarding its parameters: static (Integer::parseInt), bound (sample::sku — receiver fixed when created), unbound (Product::sku — receiver is the first parameter), constructor (Product::new). §4
Optional
A container holding one value or nothing, used as a return type to say "may be absent". Consume it with map, flatMap, filter, then orElse, orElseGet or orElseThrow. Never a field, a parameter or a collection element; never get(). §7
PECS
Producer Extends, Consumer Super. A parameter the method only reads from is List<? extends T>; one it only writes to is List<? super T>; one it does both with has no wildcard. The signature of Collections.copy. §1
Record pattern
case PercentOff(int pct) ->: a switch or instanceof pattern that tests the type and deconstructs the record's components into variables in one step. Nests — Line(Product(var sku, var p), int qty) — and runs the accessors to bind. §9
Sealed type
A class or interface whose complete set of direct subtypes is declared with permits, each of which must be final, sealed or non-sealed. Gives the compiler the closed set it needs to check a pattern switch for exhaustiveness. §9
Short-circuiting operation
A stream operation that can finish without seeing every element: limit and takeWhile among the intermediates, findFirst, anyMatch, allMatch and noneMatch among the terminals. Only laziness makes them possible. §5
Stateful operation
A stream operation that must remember earlier elements: sorted buffers everything before emitting its first element, distinct keeps a set of what it has seen. Barriers to laziness that need memory proportional to the input; put filter before them. §5
Target typing
A lambda has no type of its own; the compiler takes its parameter types and the interface it implements from the context it appears in — an assignment, a method parameter, a return. The same (a, b) -> a + b is a BinaryOperator<Integer> or a BiFunction<String,String,String>; with var it is an error. §4
Unmodifiable view
Collections.unmodifiableList(src): a wrapper that refuses writes through itself but shows whatever the underlying list currently holds. Not immutable — the source can still change. List.copyOf is the snapshot that cannot. §10
Wildcard
? in a type argument, standing for an unknown type: ? extends T (some subtype), ? super T (some supertype), or unbounded. Loosens invariance for a parameter in one direction, at the price of restrictions inside the method. Belongs in parameters, not return types. §1

Further reading

Primary sources only — the specification chapters and JEPs that define each feature, the package summaries that document the library, and the books that are actually worth the shelf space. These are links, but nothing on this page loads them; the module remains fully offline.

The Java Language Specification, SE 21

The final word on every rule in this module. Each chapter below is short enough to read in one sitting.

  • §4.10 Subtyping and §4.5.1 Type arguments — invariance, wildcards and the capture conversion behind every CAP#1 error message (§1).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-4.html
  • Chapter 5 Conversions and Contexts — the assignment, invocation and casting contexts that drive target typing and inference (§1, §4).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-5.html
  • §8.1.1.2 sealed and non-sealed classes, §8.4.3 default methods and §8.10 Record classes — the exact rules for permitted subtypes, default-method resolution and compact constructors (§3, §8, §9).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-8.html
  • §14.11 The switch statement, §14.30 Patterns and §15.28 Switch expressions — exhaustiveness, dominance and the scope of pattern variables (§9).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-14.html
  • §15.27 Lambda expressions and §15.13 Method reference expressions — what a lambda may capture, what this means inside one, and how the four reference forms are compiled (§2, §4).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-15.html

The JEPs

Each feature's design document explains the alternatives that were rejected, which is often the clearest way to understand why the rules are what they are.

  • JEP 395: Records — why accessors are name(), why there are no setters, and the "transparent carrier" phrase (§8).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/395
  • JEP 409: Sealed Classes — the permits rules and the expression-problem motivation (§9).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/409
  • JEP 441: Pattern Matching for switch and JEP 440: Record Patterns — guards, case null, dominance and nested deconstruction (§9).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/441 · https://openjdk.org/jeps/440
  • JEP 400: UTF-8 by Default — why the platform charset was a bug for twenty-five years and what changed in Java 18 (§13).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/400

Package documentation

  • java.util.stream package summary — the authoritative description of laziness, stateless versus stateful operations, non-interference and the rules for reduce and collect. Read it in full once (§5, §6).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/stream/package-summary.html
  • java.time package summary — the type matrix, the ISO calendar, and the design rationale for separating instants from local date-times (§12).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/time/package-summary.html
  • HashMap class documentation — the load-factor trade-off and the treeification note, in the JDK's own words (§11).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/HashMap.html
  • Optional class documentation — the API note stating that it is intended as a return type (§7).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Optional.html

Books

  • Effective Java, Joshua Bloch, 3rd edition — items 26 to 33 are the generics chapter (raw types, wildcards, PECS, heterogeneous containers); items 42 to 48 cover lambdas, method references and streams; item 55 is the definitive statement on Optional. Every section of this module has an item behind it.
  • Modern Java in Action, Raoul-Gabriel Urma, Mario Fusco and Alan Mycroft — the long-form treatment of streams, collectors and functional style, with the parallel-stream internals this module deferred to Java Advanced.
  • Java Generics and Collections, Maurice Naftalin and Philip Wadler — older, but still the clearest book-length explanation of wildcards, erasure and the collections framework's design.

Tools worth knowing now

Useful JDK tools for this module's material
ToolUse it to
jshellBuild a stream pipeline one operation at a time and watch what each stage emits. The fastest way to settle whether sorted comes before or after limit.
javap -p Order.classSee the members a record or inner class really has: the generated accessors and equals, the synthetic this$0 and val$base fields, and that every List<T> is a plain List.
javap -cFind the checkcast the compiler inserted at every generic read, and the invokedynamic a lambda compiles to.
javac -Xlint:all -WerrorTurn raw types, unchecked casts and missing @Override into build failures. -Xlint:rawtypes alone catches the List that should have been List<?>.
java -Dfile.encoding=…Reproduce a charset bug by running with the platform default a customer's machine has. Since Java 18 the default is UTF-8 unless you set this.
Next module

Java Advanced picks up exactly where this stops, and leaves the single-threaded world behind: threads and what they own, the Java memory model and happens-before, synchronized and ReentrantLock and how to avoid deadlock, atomics and the concurrent collections, executors and thread-pool sizing, CompletableFuture, virtual threads and structured concurrency, garbage collection and reading a GC log, class loading and initialisation order, reflection and annotations, the module system, and how to measure before optimising with JMH, JFR and the JIT's tiers. The parallel streams this module told you to measure, the ConcurrentHashMap iterators it called weakly consistent, and the enum singleton it called reflection-proof all get their explanations there.

Take the quiz above first. If you scored below 65%, the sections you missed are worth a second pass before moving on — the advanced material assumes every one of the twelve objectives, and generics, lambdas and immutability in particular are load-bearing for everything about concurrency.
